General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Scientists turned liquid carbon dioxide into an ice-like solid nearly a mile below the ocean surface

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (955 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a South China Sea trial, researchers turned liquid CO₂ into an ice-like solid that was still visible on the seabed 40 days later.
  • Nearly 1,700 meters below the South China Sea, researchers have turned liquid carbon dioxide into an ice-like solid.
  • China National Offshore Oil Corporation and Huairou Laboratory carried out the experiment in November 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a South China Sea trial, researchers turned liquid CO₂ into an ice-like solid that was still visible on the seabed 40 days later.

Nearly 1,700 meters below the South China Sea, researchers have turned liquid carbon dioxide into an ice-like solid. A mound remained visible 40 days later, offering an early test of a possible fresh carbon storage method.

China National Offshore Oil Corporation and Huairou Laboratory carried out the experiment in November 2025. Shouwei Zhou and Junlong Zhu describe it as the first exploratory sea trial of deep-water CO₂ hydrate solidification and storage.

It has been revealed that the team injected 70 tons of liquid CO₂ across two wells in the Qiongdongnan Sea Area. They wanted to see whether the deep ocean’s natural cold and pressure could help hold the carbon in solid form.

Sources indicate that capturing carbon dioxide is only part of the job. Keeping it out of the atmosphere requires somewhere to put it, with confidence that it will stay there.

Industry observers note that conventional geological storage involves injecting CO₂ underground, including into formations containing salty water. Before injection begins, engineers must assess the rock, possible escape routes, and the layers expected to seal the reservoir.

Industry observers note that the new approach seeks to reduce that dependence on geological seals. Under suitable conditions, CO₂ combines with water to form a hydrate, a solid whose water molecules enclose the gas.

It looks like ice but is neither ordinary frozen water nor dry ice. The researchers’ aim is to form this material beneath the sea and let the surrounding conditions keep it stable.

The deep ocean supplies two conditions that would otherwise have to be created: low temperatures and high pressure.

Sources indicate that those conditions favor hydrate formation. Rather than simply pumping CO₂ into a space where it remains mobile, the team wants it to accumulate as a solid.

The idea draws on work with natural gas hydrates, which contain methane. Extracting gas from those deposits means overcoming the conditions that keep them solid.

In a recent development, for carbon storage, the researchers want the opposite result. A material that stays solid and remains in place could be useful precisely because it is difficult to release.

They identify loose muddy silt and weakly cemented sand-and-mud layers as promising settings for injection and hydrate accumulation.

The operation used the “SS Amazonia” deep-water platform. Beneath it lay 1,696.5 meters of water, with the target reservoir reported at 119 meters below the seabed.

In a recent development, liquid CO₂ was injected through two wells, LS18-1-C1 and LS18-1-C2. The trial brought together drilling, injection control and underwater monitoring equipment.

During the observed release, the liquid passed through tubing and a nozzle containing several openings. The nozzle dispersed it into small droplets, helping it make contact with seawater.

White hydrate composite particles formed around the drill column. The account calls the cloud of newly formed material “ice mist”.

That was the immediate result. The follow-up inspection would show what could still be seen after several weeks in the deep sea.

Forty days later, images from a remotely operated vehicle showed an accumulated hydrate body on the bottom. Its visible height ranged from 2 to 30 centimeters above the seabed.

The researchers describe it as an artificial CO₂ hydrate “iceberg”. The name is striking, although the formation was a low mound rather than a floating mass.

Finding solid material after 40 days takes the demonstration beyond an instant of successful chemistry. It reveals that an accumulation remained visible well after injection.

In a recent development, but the images do not tell us how much of the injected CO₂ was retained in that mound or elsewhere. Nor can a 40-day observation establish whether the carbon will remain contained over much longer periods.

Those are questions for further measurements, rather than conclusions the photographs can supply.

It has been revealed that sensors near the operation measured seawater pH and CO₂ concentrations. The team reported pH holding near 7.4, without unusual spikes in carbon dioxide.

Sources indicate that the readings suggest the monitored water experienced little disturbance during the trial. Equipment mounted on the underwater vehicle helped track conditions during injection and release.

According to recent reports, that is useful evidence from a first experiment. Still, the absence of a detected change nearby is narrower than proof that the technique has no environmental impact.

Industry observers note that A larger operation would need monitoring over a wider area and a longer period. Researchers would also need to establish how the stored material behaves and whether surrounding marine life is affected.

It has been revealed that the researchers see potential savings in a method that needs fewer specific geological features. If suitable sites are widespread, finding storage locations could become easier.

They also propose reducing some of the evaluation and infrastructure demands associated with conventional storage.

For now, those are expected advantages rather than commercial results demonstrated by the trial.

Recent findings suggest that the work establishes a preliminary engineering system, including drilling in soft sediments, controlled injection and several kinds of underwater observation. It gives the team something concrete to build on.

The remaining questions concern the carbon itself: how much becomes hydrate, how much stays contained, and how conditions change with larger injections.

Costs will also have to include getting captured CO₂ to the offshore site.

It has been revealed that the seabed mound is a promising start. Turning it into dependable carbon storage will require showing that the material can hold its carbon long after the cameras leave.

The study is published in the journal ENGINEERINGenergy.

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1186 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Mindfulness training can backfire at work, and personality may explain why

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1186 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mindfulness training may increase negative feelings and rude behavior among employees who already tend to distrust and manipulate others.
  • Recent findings suggest that many companies offer mindfulness training in the hope that it will help employees manage stress, get along better and treat each other with kindness.
  • In a month-long experiment, some workers who practiced mindfulness reported more anger, disgust, and contempt toward coworkers than people with similar personalities in the other groups.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mindfulness training may increase negative feelings and rude behavior among employees who already tend to distrust and manipulate others.

Recent findings suggest that many companies offer mindfulness training in the hope that it will help employees manage stress, get along better and treat each other with kindness. But it doesn’t seem to work that way for everyone.

In a month-long experiment, some workers who practiced mindfulness reported more anger, disgust, and contempt toward coworkers than people with similar personalities in the other groups.

Workers who felt more of this hostility also reported more rudeness at work.

The pattern emerged among employees who scored high on a personality trait called Machiavellianism.

People who score high on this trait tend to distrust others and manipulate them for personal gain. Psychologists group it with two other personality traits under the name dark triad.

Previous research has linked mindfulness to greater empathy and helping coworkers. So why did these employees respond so differently?

The study was led by Adam Kay, an assistant professor in the School of Management at the University of South Florida‘s Muma College of Business.

“Mindfulness training makes us more aware of our thoughts and feelings, but that doesn’t necessarily make us better people,” Kay said.

Kay carried out the experiment at a large North American healthcare organization with 12 hospitals, 90 community health sites and 33 other workplaces.

Six hundred employees volunteered, roughly two-thirds of whom were healthcare professionals. Kay randomly divided them into three groups.

It has been revealed that the first group followed a 30-day online mindfulness program. It involved five minutes of daily instruction, along with emails and text messages reminding employees to take five mindful breaths, five times a day.

Sources indicate that the idea was simple. Notice the colors around you, listen to nearby sounds or feel your feet touching the floor. Then focus on your breathing and notice your feelings without judging them.

The second group followed a similar breathing exercise without being asked to focus on the present moment. The third group received training later.

After some employees dropped out and others failed attention checks, 473 remained in the study. Before the experiment, they had completed a personality survey containing statements such as “It’s not wise to tell your secrets.”.

Three weeks into the experiment, Kay asked employees how often they had felt anger, disgust and contempt toward their coworkers over the previous two weeks.

For people who scored low on Machiavellianism, it barely mattered which group they belonged to.

It has been revealed that things were different for those with high scores. Employees who practiced mindfulness reported stronger negative feelings than people with similar personalities in the other two groups. The difference was moderate.

Recent findings suggest that interestingly, people in both training groups felt more mindful afterward. Yet the same rise in negative feelings did not occur among those who simply practiced breathing.

Paying closer attention to their inner experiences may have made the difference.

After the program ended, employees answered another survey. This time, Kay wanted to know how they had treated their colleagues during the training.

One statement on the survey read, “I ignored or excluded a colleague from professional camaraderie.”.

Industry observers note that psychologists call these small acts of disrespect workplace incivility. They’re often subtle enough that it’s hard to tell whether someone intended to be hurtful.

The more anger, disgust and contempt employees felt, the more rude behavior they reported. This helped explain the link between mindfulness and incivility among workers with Machiavellian traits.

Sources indicate that “Workplace incivility isn’t always obvious,” Kay noted. “It usually involves subtle acts of disrespect that are easy to dismiss or deny – but that doesn’t make it harmless.”.

More obvious forms of mistreatment, such as embarrassing someone in front of other coworkers, did not follow the same pattern.

“That workplace incivility can be so damaging yet so difficult to pin on perpetrators may be precisely why it appeals to Machiavellians, who tend to be calculating and reputation-conscious,” Kay said.

Imagine working alongside someone you secretly dislike. Most days, you’re too busy answering emails, attending meetings or finishing your work to give those feelings much thought.

Sources indicate that now you spend part of every day paying attention to your thoughts and emotions. You may begin to notice just how much you dislike that person.

Kay suspects something similar happened during the experiment. Mindfulness may not have created those negative feelings. Instead, it may have made existing ones harder to ignore.

The paper even opens with a reference to philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche’s famous observation about staring into an abyss that stares back at you.

Kay considered several other possibilities. Employees were not spending more time dwelling on angry thoughts, hiding their emotions or viewing their colleagues as less than human.

Sources indicate that A bad mood didn’t explain the findings either. Neither did the other two dark triad traits, narcissism and psychopathy.

It has been revealed that this isn’t the first time researchers have discovered unexpected effects of mindfulness. Earlier research found that it can reduce people’s motivation to repair damaged relationships.

Sources indicate that machiavellianism is a personality trait that exists to varying degrees in the general population. Companies could encounter similar problems in almost any workplace.

Kay isn’t suggesting that employers abandon mindfulness training or start testing their staff for certain personality traits. Doing so could raise serious concerns about privacy, fairness and stigma.

Sources indicate that instead, companies could pay closer attention to how employees treat one another after completing a program. Lower stress and better productivity aren’t the only outcomes worth measuring.

Programs that teach compassion and ethical behavior alongside mindfulness might help. However, the people who could benefit most from such lessons may also be the least interested in taking them.

There’s an important limitation to this research. Everything Kay learned about the employees’ feelings and behavior came from the employees themselves.

In a recent development, perhaps mindfulness simply made some workers more willing to admit that they had been rude. Although Kay protected their anonymity, he cannot completely dismiss that possibility.

He considers it less likely because the pattern appeared only among workers with high Machiavellian scores who practiced mindfulness, and only for subtle acts of disrespect.

The experiment also took place at a single healthcare organization and used a commercial mindfulness program that hasn’t been independently tested.

Hospitals have strict rules about professional behavior, which may discourage more obvious forms of hostility.

According to recent reports, future studies could ask coworkers whether they noticed changes in behavior. Researchers could also observe employees directly or test different mindfulness programs.

“Mindfulness training can bring our darker feelings into sharper focus,” Kay stated. “And sometimes, it’s our coworkers who pay the price.”.

In a recent development, learning to recognize our feelings and learning to treat others better are two different things. Mindfulness may help with the first without necessarily improving the second.

The study is published in the Journal of Business Ethics.

Paul LePage, the former Maine governor who once mentioned he was “Donald Trump before Donald Trump,” is heading to Congress.

It has been revealed that the Associated Press called the race for the open 2nd District on Thursday after the Maine Secretary of State’s office tabulated the votes under the state’s ranked choice voting system. LePage ended up ahead of Democratic state Auditor Matt Dunlap 50.8 percent to 49.2 percent.

Dunlap had already conceded the race to LePage, who will succeed retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden in the sprawling district, which includes much of Maine outside the Portland and Augusta areas.

“Paul LePage is already hard at work for the people of Maine attending Congressional orientation, meeting with national leaders, and making it clear the political parties need to work together for the American people,” Brent Littlefield, a senior adviser to LePage, mentioned in a statement Thursday. “As Paul said, he will work with anyone, regardless of Party, to put Maine first.”.

According to recent reports, lePage’s win is a glimmer of good news for Republicans, who saw massive losses across the country in last week’s midterm elections. According to recent reports, lePage’s win also means that at least one Republican will continue to represent New England in Congress, taking up the mantle from Maine Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her own reelection bid last week.

Recent findings suggest that golden, who was first elected in 2018, had been a top Republican target throughout his time in Congress. But the lawmaker, known for bucking his party, proved difficult to unseat in the past two election cycles.

According to recent reports, “I also know a thing or two about winning in tough circumstances. So, I know you have to tip your hat to Paul LePage for winning in the midst of this Blue Tsunami,” Golden said in a social media post last week.

In a recent development, dunlap initially introduced his campaign as a primary challenge to Golden in the fall of 2025, only for the congressman to announce his retirement a month later. Dunlap went on to win a four-way contest for the Democratic nomination.

Tech Report: Habits like nail biting may be clues to hidden mental health struggles in teens

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1388 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • About one in eight students surveyed in England reported significant distress over nail biting, skin picking, or hair pulling.
  • Sources indicate that nail biting and skin picking are widely regarded as nothing more serious than bad habits.
  • According to recent reports, the survey was answered by 5,437 students.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

About one in eight students surveyed in England reported significant distress over nail biting, skin picking, or hair pulling.

Sources indicate that nail biting and skin picking are widely regarded as nothing more serious than bad habits. In a survey of students in England, most teens who reported these behaviors stated they caused little or no distress.

According to recent reports, the survey was answered by 5,437 students. More than half of them reported sometimes picking, pulling, or biting at their hair, skin, or nails.

The behavior was described as difficult to control, although little or no distress was reported by most of these students.

About one in eight students gave a different answer. These students said the behavior upset them quite a lot or a great deal. This distress was closely associated with anxiety, depression, and bullying.

Sources indicate that the study was led by Clare Mackay, a professor in the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Oxford. The behaviors are familiar to her from her own life.

Researchers have a name for them: body-focused repetitive behaviors, or BFRBs.

Industry observers note that “BFRBs aren’t simply bad habits. They’re often signs that a young person is struggling,” Mackay said.

Sources indicate that because the students were surveyed only once, the answers can indicate which problems occur together. The order in which those problems appeared cannot be established from the data.

The questions formed part of the 2025 OxWell Student Survey, which reached 32,102 students in England.

A total of 49 secondary schools and colleges took part, and most were state schools in Oxfordshire and Merseyside.

The survey was usually completed online during a lesson. An optional set of questions was then offered, and some students continued to it.

Within that group, the questions about picking, pulling, and biting were answered by 5,437 students aged 11 to 18.

Three questions were written for the survey by Mackay’s team. Before being sent to schools, the questions were tried by 26 people with personal experience of the behaviors. Those people also commented on the questions.

According to recent reports, in the first question, students were asked about picking, pulling, or biting at hair, skin, or nails. Only behavior that feels difficult to control was covered by this question.

Recent findings suggest that in the second question, students were asked how much the behavior upset them. Four possible answers were offered, ranging from not at all to a great deal.

The third question asked whether the behavior interfered with home life, friendships, leisure activities, or classroom learning.

According to recent reports, overall, at least one such behavior was reported by 58.5% of the students. Nail biting was the most common at 43.6%. It was followed by skin picking at 31.3% and by hair pulling at 14.5%.

For most of these students, the behavior was not experienced as a source of distress.

In a recent development, among students who reported a behavior, 35.2% stated it didn’t upset them at all. Another 42.6% said it upset them only a little. One of the two highest distress ratings was chosen by the other 22.2%.

In a recent development, the researchers then focused on that smaller group. It was made up of 691 students, or 12.7% of everyone surveyed. The highest rating was chosen by 182 of them.

Sources indicate that the lowest levels of distress were reported by students who only bit their nails. One of the two highest distress ratings was chosen by 11% of them.

In a recent development, the share was 29% among students who picked their skin. Among students who pulled their hair, a share of 37% was recorded.

Hair pulling and skin picking are listed as disorders in psychiatry’s diagnostic manuals. No separate category has been given to nail biting.

Considerable overlap between the behaviors was also observed.

It has been revealed that at least one other behavior was reported by 84% of the students who pulled their hair. Among students who picked their skin, the corresponding figure was 76%.

Industry observers note that the authors suggested that the behaviors may share one underlying process. On this account, they may not be separate conditions.

Interference with daily life was also reported more often for hair pulling than for nail biting.

Depending on the area of life, interference was reported by 5% to 13% of students who only bit their nails. For students who pulled their hair, the range was 18% to 39%.

At least one behavior was reported by 45.6% of boys and 64.6% of girls.

In a recent development, A third group consisted of 272 students who identified as trans or gender diverse, or who were unsure. Within that group, a share of 84.2% was recorded.

Recent findings suggest that distress was also lowest among boys. Distressing behaviors were reported by 5.6% of boys and 16.4% of girls. In the trans, gender-diverse, or unsure group, the figure was 25%.

The team then accounted for anxiety, depression, bullying, and age. The gaps between boys and the other two groups remained.

In a recent development, in studies of adults seen in clinics, about four women have been reported for every man with these conditions. A much smaller gap between girls and boys was observed among the students.

According to Mackay’s team, these behaviors had not previously been reported in trans and gender-diverse adolescents.

A standard 25-question checklist of anxiety and depression symptoms was also completed by the students.

Distressing behaviors were reported by 6.3% of students whose scores fell in the normal range. The share was 19.4% in the borderline range. In the highest range, which is labeled clinical by the checklist, it was 34.2%.

Distressing behaviors were also more common among students who reported bullying.

Industry observers note that among students who reported no recent bullying, 9.6% had distressing behaviors. A share of 27.1% was recorded among students bullied about once a week or more.

The team then analyzed these factors together. Anxiety and depression symptoms highlighted the strongest link to distressing behaviors. Gender and frequent bullying also remained linked.

Distressing behaviors were reported about twice as often by students who noted they had autism, ADHD, or both. The comparison was made with students who reported neither condition.

Once anxiety, depression, gender, and bullying had been accounted for, that difference was no longer statistically significant.

Sources indicate that the authors wrote that picking, pulling, and biting may work as a way of managing difficult feelings. The behaviors can then become a source of shame.

Industry observers note that young people may stay silent about the behaviors because of shame and stigma, said Polly Waite. For the same reasons, help may not be requested.

Waite is a co-author from Oxford’s Department of Experimental Psychology.

Sources indicate that that question cannot be answered by the survey. Since each student answered only once, it cannot be shown whether anxiety leads to picking and pulling.

It is also possible that anxiety is increased by the behaviors.

Earlier work suggests that the relationship may run in both directions.

The students also may not represent English teenagers as a whole. Participation in the optional questions was a matter of choice.

Compared with the full survey, this group included more girls and gender-diverse students. Higher anxiety and depression scores were recorded in it as well.

As a result, students with emotional difficulties may have been over-counted.

Recent findings suggest that the three questions are newly introduced and have not yet been formally tested. It also cannot be determined from them which students would meet the criteria for a diagnosis.

Recent findings suggest that mackay’s team wrote that these behaviors are rarely asked about in schools and clinics. A single screening question was therefore suggested by the authors.

Industry observers note that it asks whether picking, pulling, or biting upsets a young person. It also asks whether the behavior stops them from doing things they want to do.

The next question is whether distress tied to these behaviors would be eased by reducing anxiety, depression, or bullying.

The authors wrote that this could be tested in future studies, especially among girls and gender-diverse young people.

The full study was published in the journal BMJ Mental Health.

Ancient bones from two sites in northwestern Australia suggest that a varied diet gave hunters more options as rainfall and prey availability changed.

Ancient hunters in northwestern Australia ate a wide range of animals, and their leftovers suggest they could be choosy.

A study spanning roughly 50,000 years found that dietary variety could reflect plentiful food and skilled hunting.

In a recent development, the research was led by Tiina Manne from the University of Queensland. Her team examined ancient animal remains from Riwi rockshelter and Boodie Cave on Barrow Island.

It has been revealed that A widely used archaeological model predicts that hunters first concentrate on prey offering the greatest returns. They add less rewarding animals when preferred foods become harder to obtain.

The upcoming research challenges that reading of dietary diversity. At both Australian sites, people ate many kinds of animals from early in the occupation records.

“First Nations peoples in Australia were much more sophisticated and strategic in the animals they chose to hunt,” Manne noted.

“Flexibility, not fixation on a few species of prey, was the smartest way to live in an unpredictable climate.”.

Riwi stands on Gooniyandi traditional lands near the Great Sandy Desert. People began using the rockshelter about 45,000 years ago.

Its deposits contain remains of wallabies, echidnas, possums, flying foxes, lizards, and snakes. Small wallabies, lizards, and snakes dominate the earliest part of the analyzed sequence.

Boodie Cave’s first occupation dates to between about 51,100 and 46,200 years ago. Barrow Island was then part of the mainland, with its surroundings changing as sea levels fell and rose.

The team identified 1,167 specimens from Riwi and 2,083 from Boodie Cave by animal group or body size. The varied diets persisted across substantial environmental changes.

Industry observers note that burned bones and impact marks at Riwi helped link the remains to human food preparation. Some fractures also occurred while the bones were fresh.

“In a land of unpredictable rainfall, a variety of foods signal ‘plenty’, and flexibility was the best strategy,” Manne explained.

Some of the most revealing findings were bones still joined together, known as articulated remains. Their condition suggested that people had discarded body parts with little nutritional value.

“On Barrow Island, which was then connected to the mainland, the diet included wallabies, turtles and reef fish, and articulated bones suggest only the most nutritious parts were eaten and the rest were discarded,” Manne said.

“This isn’t the behavior of people short of food – they could afford to be choosy, so a broad diet reflected choice, not scarcity.”.

According to recent reports, the paper dates these articulated remains to around 7,200–6,800 years ago, long after the earliest occupation. Around this time, rising seas were cutting Barrow Island off from the mainland.

The researchers documented 24 groups of joined bones, including fish spines and parts of turtle limbs.

They interpret these discarded portions as evidence that people could select the more rewarding parts of their catches.

An animal’s value depended on more than its size. Weather affected both its condition and the effort needed to catch it.

“When water and vegetation were plentiful, large kangaroos were spread thin across the landscape, but in arid conditions they became easier to ambush as they stayed near waterholes,” Manne said.

“Small animals like bandicoots were also a good option when it got dry, because they stayed fat by switching to eating insects.”.

“Hunters who kept their options open could shift between prey as conditions changed.”.

According to recent reports, at Riwi, large kangaroo remains became prominent after about 34,000 years ago, as conditions grew drier. The authors suggest hunting them became less risky when water drew the animals into more predictable locations.

Recent findings suggest that fat mattered, too. Opened leg bones at both sites point to the extraction of marrow, while smaller insect-eating animals could retain valuable fat during drought.

Many Australian animals hide in burrows, vegetation, or rock crevices during the day. Finding them requires knowing which traces to follow.

Sources indicate that the paper draws on First Nations ecological knowledge, including signs such as fresh tracks, disturbed soil, and scratches on bark. These can reveal prey that a hunter cannot see directly.

“A tremendous amount of ecological knowledge is passed on in oral histories, including subtle signs of not only how to find prey, but the best prey depending on the season and circumstances,” Manne said.

Where hidden animals were abundant and diverse, investigating those signs could reward hunters with many different foods. A smaller animal could be a dependable catch even when a larger one promised more meat.

The authors argue that archaeological diets need to be understood through local animal behavior, food availability, and hunting costs.

A fixed ranking of desirable prey can miss how those factors change with rainfall.

Animal remains also reveal only part of a meal. Plant foods, documented at other northern Australian sites, would have supplied important carbohydrates alongside meat and fat.

“Importantly, our work suggests archaeologists around the world should re-consider how they have interpreted diet choice and diversity,” Manne concluded.

The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the Natural Academy of Sciences.

#123043. Virtual reality can make you feel sick even when the scene around you stays still

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1030 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Virtual reality can make you feel sick even when the scene around you stays still

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1030 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a five-minute VR experiment, watching a single moving ball increased nausea, eye discomfort, and disorientation as the eyes aimed and focused at different distances.
  • In a recent development, volunteers spent five minutes in a virtual reality headset watching a speckled ball glide toward them and away against a black background.
  • The ball was designed to put two jobs the eyes normally do together at odds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a five-minute VR experiment, watching a single moving ball increased nausea, eye discomfort, and disorientation as the eyes aimed and focused at different distances.

In a recent development, volunteers spent five minutes in a virtual reality headset watching a speckled ball glide toward them and away against a black background. Afterward, they reported more nausea, eye discomfort, and disorientation than before.

The ball was designed to put two jobs the eyes normally do together at odds.

As it appeared to move closer, the volunteers’ eyes turned inward to follow it, but the headset kept the image in focus at a fixed distance.

A cap of 64 electrodes recorded their brain activity shifting while it happened.

The research was conducted by Mattie Johnson, a computer science doctoral student at the University of Maryland.

Amitabh Varshney, a computer science professor and dean at the university, led the study, and Sujal Bista of the University of Maryland Institute for Health Computing was a co-author.

The team worked with the Food and Drug Administration and Sony on the study.

The team is careful about what the electrode readings mean. The scene used for comparison differed from the test scene in more than one way, and the authors can’t fully rule out eye and facial muscle activity.

So the paper calls the brain changes candidate correlates, not a signature of this kind of sickness.

Look at a real object and your eyes do two things at once: they turn inward to aim at it, and their lenses adjust to bring it into focus.

Sources indicate that the two distances agree. A headset breaks the agreement. Its screens sit at one fixed focal distance while the 3D picture asks the eyes to aim nearer or farther.

The Meta Quest 2 used here has its focal plane about 4.3 feet (1.3 meters) in front of the eyes. The team measured that with a camera and a test pattern.

Within about half a diopter of that distance the mismatch is mild. Outside it, discomfort builds.

In a recent development, so the team highlighted volunteers a black-and-white speckled ball on a black background. It glided from 11 inches (0.275 meters) out to 4.7 feet (1.425 meters) and back, one round trip every 3.9 seconds.

The ball grew as it receded and shrank as it approached, so it always looked the same size.

The researchers designed the scene to reduce the feeling that viewers themselves were moving while still making their eyes aim nearer and farther.

Forty people, 65% of them men and nearly all between 18 and 30, took part.

The researchers analyzed brain recordings from 38 people and complete questionnaires from 38 people. Each analysis excluded a different pair of participants.

Each person sat through five minutes with eyes closed, five minutes looking at a headset’s static home screen, and then five minutes of the moving ball.

It has been revealed that before and after the ball, they filled out a 1993 simulator sickness questionnaire, the SSQ. It scores nausea, eye-related symptoms, and disorientation.

According to recent reports, all three scores rose, and the total score rose by what statisticians call a large effect. Men and women both reported more symptoms, though men’s disorientation scores didn’t rise by a reliable amount.

Most participants described themselves as not at all or only slightly prone to this kind of sickness.

Sources indicate that the electrode cap sampled the scalp 250 times a second. Software stripped out blinks and muscle noise as best it could.

The team compared 50 seconds of brain activity near the end of the home-screen baseline with 50 seconds near the end of the moving-ball scene.

Industry observers note that in clusters of activity toward the front of the head, power in the fast beta and gamma brain waves fell. In clusters toward the back, power in the slower theta waves fell.

“In the frontal lobe, we found a statistically significant decrease in high brain wave frequencies during cybersickness, and in the occipital lobe we saw a statistically significant decrease in low brain wave frequencies,” Johnson mentioned.

“These changes in what we call EEG clusters could be useful predictors of a cybersickness experience.”.

The pattern is not the one Varshney’s group found in 2022 for the motion kind of virtual reality sickness, where slower waves grew stronger over the center of the head.

The studies found different patterns, but the researchers still don’t know whether the latest pattern reflects sickness, differences between the scenes, or both.

In a recent development, the baseline scene and the ball differed in brightness, content, and layout. Volunteers were told where to look during the ball but not during the baseline.

Some of the drop in slow waves at the back of the head may simply be visual processing of a different picture. The front of the head is also where eye movements leak into recordings most.

The team didn’t record whether participants wore glasses or contacts, and nearly everyone was under 30.

The authors also wrote that the headset’s three fixed lens-spacing settings fit a larger share of women than men poorly. That could add to symptoms in ways the study can’t separate.

Whether the brain changes track the sickness itself, the change of scenery, or both is the question the authors leave open.

Settling it would need a baseline scene matched to the test scene, which the authors recommend. It would also need eye tracking to remove the eyes’ own electrical traces, which Johnson’s team plans to add.

The goal beyond that is a headset that detects the pattern and adjusts the scene.

“Ultimately we want to inform technology to mitigate symptoms in real time, improving user comfort and productivity over extended periods of immersion,” Johnson stated.

Bista put it as a shift in who gets asked.

“The SSQ still has its uses, but now we have the tools to go from asking participants how they’re feeling to asking the brain and body what’s really going on,” he said.

The full study was published in the journal Virtual Reality.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • New England is the ancestral home of moderate Republicans, from the Saltonstalls to the Bushes, whose fiscal conservatism and social moderation defined the national GOP for decades.
  • Last week, Yankee Republicans suffered a near-total wipeout.
  • One Republican operative sees a path out of the wilderness in a post-Trump era.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New England is the ancestral home of moderate Republicans, from the Saltonstalls to the Bushes, whose fiscal conservatism and social moderation defined the national GOP for decades.

Last week, Yankee Republicans suffered a near-total wipeout. Maine’s Susan Collins, New England's last GOP senator, lost her seat to Democrat Troy Jackson, leaving former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, who just won a House seat, as the lone Republican headed to Congress from the region. (The picture was a bit brighter at the state level, where GOP Govs. Phil Scott of Vermont and Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire were both reelected.).

One Republican operative sees a path out of the wilderness in a post-Trump era. In an opinion piece in The Boston Globe, consultant Kristin Tate urged Fresh England Republicans to focus on fiscal discipline and recognize that “independence from national party leadership can be a political asset, not an act of betrayal.”.

After all, as the midterm election results remind us, no political realignment lasts forever.

Three decades ago, there were plenty of moderate Democrats from Southern states serving in Congress, governor’s mansions and even the White House. But in the years since Bill Clinton's exit from the political stage, Democrats have largely written off the South.

Which is partly why last week’s Democratic wins in the Carolinas, Georgia and, perhaps most notably, Mississippi were so stunning. All the elements that powered the party to victory nationally – disillusionment with Donald Trump, a rise in economic populism and hunger for change – played a role in the South as well.

But other factors were unique to a region that has seen renewed attempts to dilute Black political power with the redrawing of House districts to favor the GOP.

The Republican redistricting gambit in Southern states did not fully yield the desired results and seems to have helped galvanize Black voters and their allies, powering Democrats to unlikely victories.

It’s too soon to say whether the GOP’s reduced hold on the South represents a temporary blip or an enduring shift.

But Joe Trippi, a longtime Democratic strategist who advised candidates in Alabama and Florida this year, has a message for his party: “We need to invest in the South.”.

#MSSEN: Democrat Scott Colom defeated GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction and the first in his party to win a Senate seat in the Magnolia State since 1982.

Industry observers note that tar Heel tidal wave: Democrats in North Carolina have picked up at least five House seats, a striking development given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Prior to last week, no House Republican incumbent had lost a general election in the state since Republicans won control of the redistricting process more than a decade ago. And the Democratic gains could grow: In the 5th District, former journalist Chuck Hubbard narrowly leads 11-term Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx, and in the 3rd District, former state Rep. Raymond Smith holds a razor-thin edge over Republican Rep. Greg Murphy. The Associated Press had not called either race at publication time, though Murphy has conceded.

Sources indicate that republicans pick campaign chairs: Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno and Georgia Rep. Brian Jack will be the chairs of Republicans’ respective campaign committees for the 2028 cycle. GOP lawmakers held their leadership elections Tuesday, as our colleagues Savannah Behrmann and John T. Bennett reported. Senate Republicans are sticking with South Dakota’s John Thune to lead them in the next Congress, while House Republicans picked former Freedom Caucus Chair Jim Jordan as their leader.

Redistricting doubts: Maryland could be getting a upcoming congressional map after voters approved a constitutional amendment that would clear the way for new lines in 2028. Our colleague Victor Feldman has more on the result and other election-related ballot measures across the country. But it’s not clear how many other states may look to redistrict next cycle after Republican efforts over the past 18 months largely didn’t pay off in last week’s elections.

Run the table: With Rep. Darren Soto winning a sixth term in Florida, no Democratic incumbent lost reelection to a Republican this year. Soto’s win in a redrawn district also meant that Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had targeted under a new congressional map.

California contest: Rep. Ken Calvert defeated fellow Republican Rep. Young Kim in a rare member-versus-member contest for a redrawn Southern California seat that turned acrimonious. Republicans are poised to hold just four House seats in the Golden State after Democrats made good on five pickup opportunities under a newly introduced congressional map.

Cheesecake Factory caucus: The latest episode of the Political Theater podcast, hosted by Roll Call editor-in-chief Jason Dick, breaks down how candidates in both parties fared in counties where The Cheesecake Factory operates, after the popular chain restaurant became something of a side character in the closing weeks of the midterm campaign.

Back to school: Newly elected members of Congress are on Capitol Hill this week for freshman orientation, an experience Massachusetts Rep.-elect Dan Koh told our colleague Nina Heller is “like high school – but it’s fun high school.” The incoming lawmakers took their class photo Thursday morning and will get to pick their Capitol Hill offices after next week’s famed lottery, Nina writes.

Tracking the count: As of 4:30 p.m. Eastern time Thursday, House Democrats had flipped 44 seats, while Republicans had picked up three. Twelve races remain uncalled, including a pair in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. On the Senate side, Democrats have flipped eight seats, with only Alaska’s race still undecided.

Sources indicate that guv revision: Democrats flipped at least five governorships last week and will hold a majority of governor’s mansions next year. Two gubernatorial races remain uncalled by the AP: Kansas, where Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher is narrowly ahead of Republican state Senate President Ty Masterson, and Alaska, where Democratic former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is just below the 50 percent threshold to win the election outright. In territorial elections, Republicans flipped the governor’s office in Guam while voters in the Northern Mariana Islands will pick their next governor in a Nov. 20 runoff.

#TNSEN: Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who was elected Tennessee governor last week, is poised to pick her Senate successor. According to the Nashville Banner, the short list includes Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs, a former professional wrestler, Reps. Tim Burchett and Chuck Fleischmann, and Tennessee Deputy Gov. Stuart McWhorter.

2028 on the brain: A handful of House Democrats are already considering 2028 Senate bids, according to Axios, including Kansas’ Sharice Davids, North Carolina’s Don Davis and Pennsylvania’s Chris DeLuzio.

Senator Morrison? Minnesota Rep. Kelly Morrison is earning buzz as a potential appointee to fill the Senate seat that Democrat Amy Klobuchar is vacating to become governor, Semafor reports. House Democrats aren’t likely to be as concerned about open seats as their Republican counterparts were in recent years, given the size of the incoming Democratic majority.

In a recent development, AOC’s future: Progressive activists have released a new organization to encourage New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for president in 2028. Meanwhile, Axios reports that Ocasio-Cortez has parted ways with the digital fundraising firm she’s worked with for several years and has brought on the same firm that Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders used during his two presidential campaigns.

Recent findings suggest that women lead: Shirley Emehelu is New Jersey’s new lieutenant governor after Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill picked her to succeed Dale Caldwell, who resigned in September amid sexual harassment allegations and other ethical lapses. New Jersey is now one of five states to have women in both the governor’s and lieutenant governor’s offices, along with Massachusetts, Arkansas, Iowa and Virginia. Iowa will come off the list next year after an all-male Democratic ticket swept this year’s gubernatorial race, though five other states elected women to both offices last week.

According to recent reports, congress will once again be filled with losers – i.e, upcoming members who have lost previous bids for elected office. Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections returns to his biennial tradition as he runs down the latest list of “losers.”.

In a recent development, ducking the wave: Democrats notched significant wins in unexpected places, but one state grew redder after last week’s elections. The Fresh York Times checks in with voters in South Dakota, where the GOP won all nine statewide elections.

It has been revealed that here come the MBAs: Democrats with corporate connections were among the winners in last week’s elections, countering the idea that candidates with serious business credentials have struggled within the party, The Wall Street Journal reports. Industry observers note that was it necessary? California redrew its congressional map to favor Democrats in response to Texas taking a similar step to boost the GOP. But some are questioning whether the state needed to cast aside its independent redistricting commission to rejigger the lines, given the scale of Democrats’ wins. “What they were literally saying is, ‘Let’s undo democracy to protect democracy,’” Lincoln Project co-founder Mike Madrid told CalMatters. “There’s something very Orwellian about it.”.

Song of the cycle: The Latest York Times reviews “Talafreako,” an unlikely viral anthem celebrating the newly elected Democratic senator from Texas.

The man behind the grill: The New York Times profiles Russ Hudson, the Mississippi man in Colom’s now-legendary “Pick another protein” ad.

That was the last time Democrats won 11 House seats in North Carolina.

As of Thursday afternoon, they appear on track to match that number. They’ve already won nine seats – a mark they last cleared in the 1982 midterms – and they’re narrowly ahead in two more races.

Recent findings suggest that if those leads hold, Democrats' 11-member delegation would look much different than the one sworn in some 66 years ago in 1961. Tar Heel Democrats taking office in January would include four women, six Black members and one Hispanic member.

In 1950, Michigan beat Ohio State in the Snow Bowl without a first down, and the blizzard behind it dumped up to 62 inches of snow

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1168 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Snow Bowl storm, later called the Great Appalachian Storm, contributed to at least 160 deaths and is the worst Ohio Valley snowstorm NOAA has analyzed.
  • Recent findings suggest that on the Saturday after Thanksgiving in 1950, Ohio State and Michigan played their annual game in Columbus in a blizzard.
  • It did so without a single first down and without completing a pass, according to the National Weather Service.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Snow Bowl storm, later called the Great Appalachian Storm, contributed to at least 160 deaths and is the worst Ohio Valley snowstorm NOAA has analyzed.

Recent findings suggest that on the Saturday after Thanksgiving in 1950, Ohio State and Michigan played their annual game in Columbus in a blizzard. At noon, the temperature at the city’s airport, a few miles from Ohio Stadium, was 10°F, and visibility was half a mile.

Michigan won 9-3. It did so without a single first down and without completing a pass, according to the National Weather Service. The game became known as the Snow Bowl, and some call it the Blizzard Bowl.

Sources indicate that the storm that buried the field was much bigger than one football game. Over the following days, it dropped as much as 62 inches of snow in West Virginia, sent temperatures down to 3°F in Atlanta, and pushed hurricane-force gusts into the Northeast.

It ranks as the worst Ohio Valley snowstorm analyzed by scientists at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

The game’s place in history has little to do with the quality of the football, the weather service’s office in Wilmington, Ohio, says.

It is remembered for “the weather, as the game was played in a significant blizzard unlike any that either school had played in before, or since.”.

Neither team could move the ball, so they kept punting it away. Michigan punted 24 times, and its total offense for the whole game was 27 yards. Ohio State punted 21 times, and four of those punts were blocked by the Wolverines.

All of the scoring came from blocked kicks. Ohio State blocked a punt that led to a field goal. Two of Michigan’s blocks led to a safety and a touchdown.

“It speaks to the severity of the storm, the remarkable conditions, and just how debilitating extreme weather can be,” the Wilmington office wrote.

Industry observers note that the weather service has analyzed the afternoon’s hourly observations at Port Columbus Airport. The temperature climbed only from 10°F at noon to 16°F at 4 p.m.

According to recent reports, sustained winds blew at 17 to 22 mph, with gusts of more than 35 mph, so wind chills stayed between -8°F and -1°F. Visibility dropped as low as a quarter of a mile in snow and blowing snow.

Sources indicate that two days earlier, the weather had been very different. On Thursday evening, November 23, which was Thanksgiving Day, it was 39°F in Columbus at 8 p.m.

An arctic cold front then moved through, and by midnight it was 20°F. By 7 a.m. on Friday, the temperature had fallen to 8°F.

In a recent development, on the day of the game, 7.5 inches of snow fell on Columbus. The weather service states that is still the city’s record for a single November day.

From Thursday night to the following Tuesday, the city got 14.9 inches. Its November 1950 total of 15.2 inches remains the snowiest November on record there.

The cold front that arrived on Thanksgiving night was the precursor to the Great Appalachian Storm of 1950.

According to the weather service office in Jackson, Kentucky, the arctic air behind it sent temperatures to all-time November lows across the Upper Midwest and the Ohio Valley.

Chicago dropped to -2°F on November 24, tying its lowest November reading, and the next day Louisville hit -1°F and Lexington -3°F, both records for the month.

On November 25, low pressure formed over the Carolinas, the Jackson office says. It moved northwest into Ohio by the middle of the next day, spreading heavy snow as it went, then spun over Lake Erie before it weakened and left for Canada on November 29 and 30.

The snow piled up from western Pennsylvania deep into West Virginia. Several places received more than 50 inches, and Coburn Creek, West Virginia, reported the largest total, 62 inches, according to NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI). Pittsburgh got about 30 inches.

Industry observers note that the cold reached far into the South. Temperatures fell to 22°F in Pensacola, Florida, 5°F in Birmingham, Alabama, 3°F in Atlanta and 1°F in Asheville, North Carolina, NCEI notes, and the record cold damaged crops in Georgia and South Carolina.

In a recent development, the storm drew arctic air in on one side and warm Atlantic air in on the other. While Pittsburgh was buried under snow at single-digit temperatures, Buffalo, New York, about 200 miles to the north, had temperatures in the 40s and no snow at all, the Jackson office says.

In the Northeast, the problem was wind. Newly introduced York City recorded a gust of 94 mph, and Newark, New Jersey, 108 mph. Bear Mountain, just north of New York City, had a 140 mph gust, and Mount Washington in New Hampshire reached 160 mph.

The winds caused extensive tree damage and power outages, and coastal flooding that broke through dikes at LaGuardia Airport and flooded its runways.

Fierce winds are still a feature of substantial East Coast storms, as earth.com saw when blizzard winds battered the coast in a more recent storm.

Heavy rain on the warm side of the storm brought near-record flooding to eastern Pennsylvania. Then, in the first week of December, unusually warm weather melted the snow rapidly. The Ohio River rose to 28.5 feet in Pittsburgh and 56 feet in Cincinnati, 4 feet above flood stage in both cities.

Recent findings suggest that the storm contributed to at least 160 deaths, NCEI says. Insurance companies paid out more for its damage than for any earlier storm or hurricane, according to the Jackson office. They call it the costliest storm on record up to that time. NCEI describes it as one of the costliest storms on record.

NCEI rates major snowstorms with its Regional Snowfall Index, which combines how much snow fell, how large an area it covered and how many people lived there.

According to recent reports, the 1950 storm scored 34.7 in the Ohio Valley, the highest of the 232 storms analyzed there. The second-worst, in March 1993, scored 24.6. In that region, more than 6.1 million people lived where at least 18 inches of snow fell.

In the Northeast, it ranks ninth of 230 storms, just behind the storms of February 2003, February 2010 and January 2016.

Scientists are still studying how storms like this work. NASA-backed scientists have flown research planes straight into snowstorms to learn how their heaviest bands of snow form.

In a recent development, the information was obtained from the National Weather Service’s pages Snow Bowl – November 25, 1950 (Wilmington, Ohio) and The Great Appalachian Storm of 1950 (Jackson, Kentucky), from NOAA NCEI’s article The Great Appalachian Storm in Historical Context, and the Michigan vs. Ohio State team game records of the University of Michigan’s Bentley Historical Library and the Ohio State University Archives.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Generators come in all sizes, but when you need power for camping or tailgating, or to power tools when you’re too far from an outlet, a large one meant for home backup is just too much.
  • When you’re shopping for a portable generator, there are a few important things to consider, including power, weight, and fuel type.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Generators come in all sizes, but when you need power for camping or tailgating, or to power tools when you’re too far from an outlet, a large one meant for home backup is just too much. Power stations are handy, but once they run out of power, they take a long time to recharge. That’s where a smaller-sized portable generator can really shine. So long as you have the fuel, they can keep running.

When you’re shopping for a portable generator, there are a few important things to consider, including power, weight, and fuel type. For portable power, models that output 2,000 to 5,000 watts will generally be simple enough to lift in and out of a truck, though some models that generate more are designed to be lightweight. Anything over 100 pounds starts to buck the idea of something being portable, even if it has wheels.

Sources indicate that fuel type matters, too. All generators run on gas, but dual-fuel models can also run on propane. The drawback is that propane delivers slightly less power output and shorter running time, but it runs a lot cleaner and is much less messy to deal with.

It has been revealed that if you’re powering sensitive electronics like digital equipment or TVs, you’ll also want to look for an inverter generator, which delivers more stable “cleaner” power that won’t damage your gear. They also run quieter than standard models. For these reasons, all of the picks on our list are inverter generators.

Recent findings suggest that keeping portability in mind, the models we cover in this story are all 7,500 watts and under. For the models that we tested, we based our methods on our experience using generators for backup power with and without transfer switches, on construction sites to run power tools and equipment, as well as running sound systems and lighting at outdoor events. We measured the sound levels of these generators idling with no load, and while running under load at two feet and 25 feet. We then used an oscilloscope to observe the sine wave of the alternating current generated by these machines, and a clamp meter to check voltage output.

Some examples of devices we used with large starting and running loads include a large air conditioner and a portable table saw. In one case, we even tested it paired to a solar inverter-charger. We evaluated these generators based on ease of starting, power response, sound levels, value, safety, and reliability to select the top performers.

Sources indicate that the Honda EU2200i inverter generator has just about everything you want from a portable generator. It’s half the size and weight of comparable generators in its class; it’s very quiet and clean when operating; and it’s fully enclosed so you can rapidly and easily transport it and move it around without worrying about it getting caught on anything.

It has been revealed that that enclosure is an vital feature, as it protects the inverter electronics and helps contain noise—the EU2200i is remarkably quiet. In testing, we measured sound levels of 68.9 decibels at the generator under no load. When we switched it to “eco” mode, which reduces engine speed when power isn’t called for, the sound was reduced to 76 decibels.

Sources indicate that when we used an oscilloscope to look at the sine wave of the current generated, the curves were smooth and symmetrical, an indicator of “clean” power. This remained true even when running heavy loads from devices like a table saw or an air conditioner.

There are some nice design features, too. The vent on the gas cap closes so fumes or fuel cannot escape. You could breathe freely packing this in the passenger compartment of an SUV. Likewise, the power on/off switch doubles as a fuel shutoff, so it can’t be forgotten.

Recent findings suggest that lastly, the EU2200i has ports for parallel operation. With the correct cable kit, it connects to a second EU2200i to double the output to 4,400 starting and 3,600 running watts. The EU2200i is ideal for camping and other outdoor events where generator noise might be frowned on.

Sources indicate that we like the GD400BN because it’s powerful, quiet, and portable at a reasonable price point. The interesting thing about this inverter generator is how much power it can deliver, yet it’s still as compact as similar generators that deliver half as much output. Even when running on lower-output propane as the fuel source, it can run up to 3,000 watts, which is considerable for a generator that only weighs 47 pounds.

Industry observers note that another plug or two would’ve been nice, however. Its single AC outlet limits you to plugging one power tool or appliance at a time, despite having enough output to power more than one device. It does have a 120-volt, 30-amp outlet for connecting to an RV, though, so that does make up for it a bit, but only if you have that need. The 1.1-gallon fuel tank is also a bit limiting regarding runtime for gasoline, but that’s easily overcome by using propane. For all intents and purposes, this is a very nice dual-fuel generator, and at a list price of $600, it comes at a reasonable price to boot.

The Wen DF360iX offers a considerable amount of utility for an affordable price. You have the option to run the generator on gasoline or propane with a running output of up to 2,900 watts. While propane delivers a bit less at 2,600 watts, that’s plenty of power for a job site or camping use and even enough electricity for small to midsize RVs.

Recent findings suggest that while this generator is fairly light at 49 pounds, it doesn’t cut back on ports, including a 30-amp port for direct connection to an RV. There are also two three-prong AC ports, a 12-volt DC receptacle, and two USB-A ports. Like most inverter generators, it produces less noise. This model is rated at around 65 decibels of noise at a quarter load, which is quiet enough that it shouldn’t bother the neighbors. There are some nice safety features, too, including auto-shutoff if the fuel runs too low and a carbon monoxide (CO) sensor that detects if dangerous levels are present.

Of course, with any generator in this price range (under $500), there are compromises. This model has a pretty small fuel tank—only 1.5 gallons—so you won’t be able to run this on gasoline for long periods (around five hours with a half-load) without having to stop and refill. You can mitigate this, however, by relying on a larger tank of propane. For example, a 20-pound tank should enable you to run it for up to 14 hours.

According to recent reports, GENERATOR SAFETYWhile not hard to run, generators present dangers, so you need to follow basic safety rules. Never operate them in a closed space, like a garage or shed. Exhaust gases contain carbon monoxide (CO), a lethal, odorless, colorless gas. Most manufacturers offer models that shut down when they detect carbon monoxide building up. Do not run a generator in a garage with the door open, or in front of the garage with the door open, because carbon monoxide can still get trapped and seep into the house. Run generators at least 20 feet away, including from windows and doors, with the exhaust blowing away from the house.

It has been revealed that RV owners need a generator outfitted with at least a 120-volt, 30-amp outlet, but it also helps to have a decent amount of power to go with it, so that you can run things like a heater or an air conditioner. This model from Champion offers both, with the outlet and up to 3,500 running watts, which is enough to power a small- to medium-sized RV.

It also offers great fuel flexibility. With a full 2.3-gallon fuel tank, it should be able to run for up to 14 hours, but it’s dual-fuel, so with a full 20-pound propane tank, this generator can supply 21 hours of uninterrupted power.

In addition to being a solid companion for camping and RVing, this generator could serve as a useful tool in an emergency at home where power is needed. Using a manual transfer switch, you could power a few 120-volt circuits using the 30-amp connection. And the inverter will help to keep it running more quietly, which is helpful at home or the campground.

According to recent reports, one of our test editors picked up this generator when faced with a home emergency where he needed a generator with specific features, promptly, and on a budget. A failed generator at a solar-powered off-grid cabin necessitated the quick acquisition, and, happily, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel Inverter Generator showed up on the doorstep in only two days.

Industry observers note that in about 15 minutes, with minimal assembly and after adding oil, the generator was connected to a propane cylinder by a hose and was running on the first cycle of the starter. Since then, it’s run steadily at 500 watts, up to 5,500 watts, at 240 volts (great for powering high-voltage appliances like dryers or water pumps), to charge a battery bank during the winter when sunlight wasn’t enough to get the job done.

This Pulsar puts out very clean power, too, with a claimed total harmonic distortion (THD) of less than 3 percent, which met the requirements of the solar inverter-charger it was paired with.

According to recent reports, using the inverter to monitor the current frequency, we found that it was indeed very stable with minimal variance, between 59.97 and 60.09 Hz. All things considered, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel is a good value for the specs, capacity, and features.

Generac’s iQ3800 Portable Inverter Generator is a great example of what we love about dual-fuel, inverter generators. This type of generator can deliver cleaner power than a standard model, meaning there’s less distortion in the electrical current frequency. That’s ideal for powering sensitive electronics, such as TVs, computer equipment, and smart household appliances. This is also a closed-frame inverter generator, which tends to be quieter; the iQ3800 is one of the quietest generators we’ve tested of this size.

Sources indicate that we were very impressed with how easy the iQ3800 is to operate. The electric start and auto choke worked perfectly, taking only about four to five seconds, while the manual pull-start also fired up the generator with minimal effort. Switching between fuel types was also very simple to perform. Once running, you can view crucial information on an easy-to-read LED display that lists the total hours the machine has run, the fuel level for the gasoline tank (there’s no gauge for propane), and a load gauge that uses a bar graph to show power output level—knowing that helps to avoid overloading the generator.

Recent findings suggest that the inverter technology might be the most important feature of the iQ3800. This generator has a total harmonic distortion (THD)—a level of variance in the current frequency—of less than 3 percent, which is very low. Essentially, anything with a screen or any smart device would be best powered using an inverter generator like the iQ3800. It’s an ideal generator to power RVs in campgrounds or off-grid, and a great option for emergency backup in urban areas.

Full Generac iQ3800 Portable Inverter Generator Review.

These generators, sometimes called backup generators, are used to provide temporary power when and where it is needed. Portable is a relative term; some are more portable than others. While the smallest models can be picked up and carried, most have wheels and a handle to make transport easier. However, at 100 pounds or more, picking them up to load or move may take two people. Appliances, power tools, or other devices can be plugged directly into standard outlets on the generator’s front panel.

Additionally, many models have a twist-lock plug that can provide up to 240 volts and be used to power circuits in a home via a manual transfer switch. You may hear generators like these referred to as “open frame” generators, which simply means that the engine, fuel tank, and generator components are not enclosed in bodywork.

Though inverter-type generators are—like their standard cousins—typically portable, we group them separately because they’re significantly and technically different in terms of how they work.

Like most generators, inverter generators provide 120/240 volts of AC power. They generate AC current just like the others, but it’s then converted to DC (Direct Current), and then inverted back to AC. The conversion and inversion is controlled by circuitry which acts like a filter, flattens surges, and cleans up the sine wave (or oscillating wave) of the electrical current.

Typical generators have varying degrees of distortion in the sine wave of the alternating current. This isn’t usually an glitch for most electrical devices, though sensitive electronics like tablets, laptops, televisions, and other smart devices can be damaged by current distortion or surges. These devices will last longer with “clean” power and steady voltage. Because of that added complication, inverter generators can be significantly more expensive.

According to recent reports, standby generators are permanently installed and connected to a home. These may power selected, critical circuits during a power outage, or may provide power for the whole home. Standby generators have systems that monitor power supplied by a utility and start automatically in the event of an outage. Since they’re not portable or easily moved, we didn’t include any here.

Sources indicate that it’s crucial to know what you intend to power with a generator in order to choose the right size. Manufacturers list two figures for generators: starting watts and running watts. Starting watts include the initial surge required to start appliances or tools with powerful electric motors or compressors. Once started, these devices require far less power to run continuously.

In a recent development, many manufacturers have a chart with estimated power requirements for common appliances and tools to help you figure out what you need. For a more precise measurement, you can also calculate the figure yourself by adding up the power consumption of specific appliances and adding them together.

To calculate watts, multiply voltage (usually 120 volts) by the amps (amperage) required to run the appliance (usually found on a tag attached to the appliance). Do this for each item that the generator will power.

Recent findings suggest that most portable generators are powered by gasoline, the most commonly available fuel. However, when using generators for emergency power, their infrequent use presents some issues to consider.

The first is that when massive, catastrophic storms hit and power outages last for days, gas stations may struggle to meet demand, resulting in long lines. The second concern has to do with the infrequent use of backup generators, which may sit for months to years between uses.

Industry observers note that gasoline sitting in a carburetor will slowly evaporate over time, leaving gummy deposits that can block fuel from getting through, making it difficult or even impossible to start your generator without servicing. You can avoid this by closing the fuel valve and letting the generator run until it stalls, using up the remaining fuel in the carburetor. Also, over time, gasoline can oxidize or become “stale,” losing combustibility. It may also absorb water, which can then corrode fuel tanks and other metal components in the fuel system. Starting a generator regularly, as well as treating fuel with a stabilizer, can help fight these issues.

Ethanol-free gasoline, available at some gas stations, is also less susceptible to degradation over time than standard 87-octane pump gas; however, it’s still a good idea to mix the fuel going into your generator with stabilizer.

It has been revealed that dual-fuel generators can run on gasoline or liquified petroleum gas (LPG), commonly known as propane. Switching between the fuels is simple, and you won’t be tied to the availability of one type of fuel.

Sources indicate that A significant advantage of propane is that it’s very stable when stored for long periods of time. It won’t go stale, and it won’t gum up carburetors from sitting. Plus, some homes that use propane for other purposes may already have large storage tanks on the premises, foregoing the need to make repeated trips out for fuel.

According to recent reports, the downside to propane is that it creates fewer BTUs (British Thermal Units, a measurement of energy) than the same amount of gasoline. So, a generator running on propane will have slightly reduced starting and running watts. On the plus side, though, it will also run a little quieter than those that run on gasoline.

In a recent development, while not as common, tri-fuel generators add an option to connect by natural gas. Some propane-powered generators can be converted to run on natural gas, as well. Like propane, natural gas can run cleaner and a little quieter. However, it also creates fewer BTUs than gasoline and propane, so it will also produce reduced starting and running watts.

Natural gas also requires a dedicated line for the generator, which most homes that have access to natural gas will not have, and thus will need to be professionally installed.

If you’re powering appliances, tools, or other devices by plugging them directly into the standard outlets on the generator, the answer is no. If the generator is being used to power circuits in your home, maybe. It’s always best to consult the operator’s manual, a licensed electrician, or your local building officials about township ordinances—some localities may have requirements that differ from the National Electrical Code (NEC).

Electrical circuits need to be grounded to operate devices safely, so that any current that shorts out or has a fault is directed to the ground, i.e., the actual, literal earth, so the user doesn’t become the conduit to “ground.”.

Sources indicate that there are two ways that generators are grounded: neutral-bonded and floating neutral. Neutral-bonded means the neutral wire is connected (i.e., bonded) to the generator frame. With a floating neutral, the neutral is not connected to the frame. In the latter case, the generator should be grounded by connecting the ground terminal to a grounding rod driven into the ground.

Generators with ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) outlets, when used to power circuits in your home, require neutral switching and a manual transfer switch, and must be grounded by connecting the ground terminal to a ground rod driven into the soil. Neutral-switching transfer switches are also referred to as three-pole transfer switches.

There could be numerous reasons for difficulty starting a generator. The first things to check are whether or not there's any fuel in the tank, and if the fuel valve is turned open. Then, check for any obstructions in the air cleaner box. If that’s clean, move on to check that the engine has spark.

If your generator has sat for a long time without treated fuel, the carburetor may be clogged up and require cleaning—if you’re unfamiliar with any of these steps, it may be best to take it to a shop for service.

In an emergency, use what you can get, but as a general rule, 87 octane fuel will be fine—just don’t go lower than that.

As long as we’re talking fuel, it’s always best to use ethanol-free fuel in equipment with small gas engines—if that’s not possible, nothing more than 10-percent ethanol. Ethanol can attract moisture, which will then separate and settle in the gas tank or carburetor, where it can corrode and clog the fuel system. For this reason, it’s also a good idea to treat gas with a fuel stabilizer.

Much like your lawn mower, generators need regular maintenance. However, since they often see less use, maintenance intervals tend to be farther apart. Typical maintenance would include changing oil, checking the air filter and changing it if needed, changing the fuel filter if so equipped, and checking the spark plug.

The best source of specific maintenance and troubleshooting information for your generator is the owner’s manual.
