Tech Report: Would we know if lab-grown brain tissue became conscious?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (869 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists propose testing whether lab-grown brain tissue can learn a pattern and detect when it changes, a possible clue in the search for signs of consciousness.
  • Scientists can grow small clusters of human brain cells in a dish.
  • Industry observers note that two neuroscientists have now proposed a way to check what such tissue, called a brain organoid, can do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists propose testing whether lab-grown brain tissue can learn a pattern and detect when it changes, a possible clue in the search for signs of consciousness.

Scientists can grow small clusters of human brain cells in a dish. One set of joined clusters has reacted to capsaicin, the compound found in chili peppers, but a reaction like that doesn’t show the tissue feels anything.

Industry observers note that two neuroscientists have now proposed a way to check what such tissue, called a brain organoid, can do. Their proposal borrows tests already used on infants, sleeping people, and patients who can’t respond.

The tests ask whether an organoid can learn a pattern and notice when the pattern is broken. The proposal reports no results, and the authors wrote that it is highly unlikely today’s organoids are conscious.

Lucia Melloni of Ruhr University Bochum in Germany and Stanislas Dehaene of the Collège de France in Paris wrote the proposal. Both belong to a brain and consciousness research program at CIFAR, a Canadian research organization.

“I don’t believe that brain organoids right now possess consciousness,” Melloni said.

Sources indicate that “But given the pace with which the technology is advancing, they may do so in future. That’s why we need to start thinking about how we can find out.”.

Industry observers note that organoids are grown from human stem cells. The cells organize themselves into tiny tissues that copy some features of the early developing brain.

It has been revealed that researchers can also fuse several organoids into what they call an assembloid. The one that reacted to capsaicin joined four organoids to rebuild a basic pain pathway.

“A reaction, however, is not proof that the tissue feels anything,” Melloni said.

Sources indicate that other teams have wired brain cells into machines, including one hooked to a simplified version of the video game Pong. Melloni and Dehaene wrote that those setups are too complex to show what the living tissue itself worked out.

In a 2024 study they cited, a gel that responds to electricity produced similar results in place of the cells.

The central test comes from research on how people process sequences.

Sources indicate that A person hears ba-ba-ba-ba-bu again and again. The brain reacts to the bu because it differs from the four sounds before it.

Sources indicate that after many repeats, the person learns the whole pattern. If the sequence then comes as ba-ba-ba-ba-ba, the brain reacts again, this time because the expected bu is missing.

The second reaction is the harder one. It depends on a memory of the whole sequence, built up over many repeats.

An organoid has no ears, so researchers would use electrical pulses or light in place of sounds.

They would stimulate two or more separate groups of cells in sequence and record how the tissue’s activity changes.

The question would be whether the same sequence produces a different response depending on what came before it.

Monkeys can learn patterns like this one too. That has let researchers study the brain activity behind the reactions in animals that have no language.

Recent findings suggest that in people, the first kind of reaction survives sleep and anesthesia. The second seems to require a person to be awake and paying attention.

Sources indicate that doctors have also tried the test on patients who can’t communicate. In those patients, 80% of the ones whose brains demonstrated the second reaction later regained consciousness.

In a recent development, the test missed many others. Only 35% of the patients who recovered had shown the reaction.

Recent findings suggest that melloni and Dehaene wrote that no single test would be enough. Their confidence would rise if an organoid passed this test along with several other known signs of consciousness.

In a recent development, the authors wrote that a failed test is perhaps the more likely outcome. A failure would lower confidence that an organoid is conscious.

Industry observers note that dehaene has a financial interest in this kind of testing. He is a co-inventor on a patent for methods to monitor consciousness and an associate at a company that uses those methods in clinics.

Industry observers note that the authors wrote that there is no evidence current organoids hold any rich picture of the outside world or of themselves. The tissues are tiny, and they are cut off from a body and from surroundings.

Organoids can be kept alive for months to years, though, and they keep changing as they age. The authors proposed running the same tests on an organoid again and again as it matures.

Human babies show the second kind of reaction at 3 months of age, and it may be present before birth, after 35 weeks of pregnancy.

Repeated testing would show when each ability appears in an organoid.

The authors also wrote that if several signs ever pointed the same way, the ethical treatment of these tissues should change with the evidence.

Melloni and other researchers have called for an international board to oversee organoid research.

The full study was published in the journal Neuron.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A group of prominent Senate Democrats is pushing to use a must-pass spending bill to cut off funding for the Iran war, complicating the path toward a bipartisan deal for averting a partial government shutdown next month.
  • Tim Kaine, D-Va., remarked Thursday he is working on legislative language ending the war that he wants attached to the next continuing resolution that is needed by Dec.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., talks with reporters in the Capitol on Sept. 30. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

A group of prominent Senate Democrats is pushing to use a must-pass spending bill to cut off funding for the Iran war, complicating the path toward a bipartisan deal for averting a partial government shutdown next month.

Recent findings suggest that sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., remarked Thursday he is working on legislative language ending the war that he wants attached to the next continuing resolution that is needed by Dec. 11, when current funding runs out.

“I know it’s going to be my main push,” he said. “I have to work with colleagues to try to find some language that works. And I’m not there yet, but I’ve told everybody that’s an opportunity.”.

Democratic Sens. Michael Bennet of Colorado, Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, Tammy Duckworth of Illinois and independent Bernie Sanders of Vermont released a statement Thursday that they would oppose any deal that does not include “language that restricts the Trump Administration from using appropriated funds to continue his war against Iran.”.

In a recent development, “When we vote on appropriations, we intend to fund the government and stop funds for this war,” the senators mentioned. “It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve.”.

It is unlikely that Republicans, who are in control of both chambers of Congress until January, not to mention the Oval Office beyond that, would agree to such a deal.

House Appropriations Chairman Tom Cole, R-Okla., said earlier this week that “a Republican Congress is not going to send bills to a Republican president that he's going to veto.”.

While ending the war is a top priority of Democrats as they take back power in the fresh Congress, insisting on doing so this year could lead to a Christmas-time partial government shutdown. If a shutdown starts after Dec. 11, it’s possible it would still be ongoing when Democrats take control of both chambers in January.

But some Democrats appeared to still be weighing how swiftly to push for a cutoff of war funding.

Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash, stated that whether or not Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth remains in his job, “we’re still going to have language stopping this war.”.

She was coy on whether that fight would take place on the anticipated continuing resolution in December or wait until next year when Democrats take back power, saying that lawmakers are “looking at all options.”.

In a recent development, democrats are committed to ending the "reckless and costly war of choice in Iran," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., stated Thursday. He deferred to House Appropriations ranking member Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., "to see what’s possible in advance of Dec. 11" in talks with the other top appropriators.

"I don’t want to get out ahead of Congresswoman DeLauro, but House Democrats have uniformly opposed providing any additional money to Donald Trump’s war machine. to Pete Hegseth’s war machine, over in the Middle East," Jeffries noted.

It’s not clear how long a potential continuing resolution would last, and DeLauro said earlier this week that she wants it to be as short as possible.

The Office of Management and Budget has not yet submitted “anomalies” — changes to the current spending levels to be included in the continuing resolution — to Congress.

The administration is considering options including a stopgap bill that would run through March, sources familiar with the talks said. But no decision on the timing covered by the anomalies has been made.

Aris Folley, Jacob Fulton and Michael Macagnone contributed to this report.

#123035. A morning dose of blue light may help you sleep better at night

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (950 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

A morning dose of blue light may help you sleep better at night

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (950 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Office workers given morning blue light for 30 minutes slept about 11 minutes longer that night and brought more energy to work the next day.
  • Blue light has become the villain of bedtime.
  • Yet the same light, delivered for half an hour after waking, made a group of office workers sleep longer and better that night.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Office workers given morning blue light for 30 minutes slept about 11 minutes longer that night and brought more energy to work the next day.

Blue light has become the villain of bedtime. Phones get dimmed at night and glasses that block it sell as sleep aids.

Yet the same light, delivered for half an hour after waking, made a group of office workers sleep longer and better that night. The gain carried into the next day’s work.

The effect was modest, about 11 minutes more sleep a night and a small lift in how well people mentioned they slept.

Participants who reported sleeping better also reported more alertness and less mental fatigue the next day. Greater alertness was linked to more engagement at work.

Kathleen Keeler, who studies management and human resources at Ohio State University’s Fisher College of Business, led the study.

Christopher Barnes of the University of Washington’s business school and Brian Gunia of Johns Hopkins University’s Carey Business School were among her co-authors.

The glasses came from a manufacturer called Ayo, which donated half the pairs used.

Sources indicate that barnes stated the mechanism is not a morning jolt from the blue light itself. “It’s that the blue light helps them sleep better later that night, which helps them the following day,” he noted.

The body runs on a roughly 24-hour cycle that decides when a person feels sleepy and when they feel awake.

Light is the strongest signal that keeps that internal clock on time, and blue light, in particular, is what the clock responds to most.

Blue light at night pushes the clock later and holds back melatonin, the hormone that brings sleep on.

That is the part everyone has heard. The same light in the morning pulls the clock earlier, which, in principle, should make sleep come sooner and run smoother that night.

Workplace researchers had tested the night half of that idea with blue-blocking glasses and found better sleep and better work. Workplace studies had not tested the morning half.

The team invited 200 full-time employees at a large Midwestern university, all working roughly nine to five, and 182 finished the study.

Sources indicate that nearly three in four were women, and the typical participant was in their early forties. They had been with the university for about a decade on average.

Recent findings suggest that for 10 workdays, each wore glasses that shine blue-turquoise light toward the eyes for 30 minutes right after waking, between 5 and 10 a.m. On average they started just before 7 a.m.

Sources indicate that for one of the two weeks the blue glasses ran at full power. For the other they ran at 1%, a glow so faint that in earlier tests people couldn’t tell the two settings apart.

Which week came first was decided at random, so every person served as their own comparison.

Participants filled in a survey each morning about the night’s sleep and their energy, and another each afternoon about their work, from engagement to helping coworkers to slacking off.

The team collected 1,259 daily surveys and registered its predictions in advance.

Each participant kept the glasses and a year of the companion app afterward.

After a full-power morning, people reported sleeping about 11 minutes longer that night, and rated the night’s sleep about 3.5% higher. Neither number is large. The team then traced the effect through the next day.

Longer and better sleep predicted more alertness the next day, and better sleep predicted less of the feeling that one’s mental energy is running low.

Sources indicate that alertness, in turn, predicted stronger work engagement and more helping behavior. Less depletion predicted better task performance and fewer behaviors like taking an overlong break.

Each link in that chain was small, and the team said so.

“This is a pretty small, cheap, easy intervention, and we’re getting meaningful movement on work outcomes that matter,” Barnes mentioned.

The morning blue light didn’t increase alertness that same day.

Alertness that same day was no higher, which is why the authors read the whole effect as running through sleep.

The benefit also built across the week rather than appearing in full on day one.

According to recent reports, two groups gained more than the rest. People who arrived with existing sleep problems saw a bigger improvement in sleep quality.

Younger employees saw a bigger gain in sleep length, with effects on engagement and helping that the older workers did not show.

The authors tied the age gap to the eye’s declining sensitivity to light with age, and called both findings exploratory.

It has been revealed that barnes had a cheaper suggestion. “The best thing you could do in the morning is get outside,” he remarked.

Every measure here was self-reported, including how well people said they performed, so the findings wait on a replication with objective records.

According to recent reports, everyone studied worked daytime hours at one university, and most were women. The authors noted shift workers, who often miss morning light altogether, might gain more, but no one in this study worked nights.

The measure of workplace misbehavior was also short and noisy, which the authors stated may have hidden a larger effect rather than created a false one.

What the glasses add on top of a sunny walk is the open question, since the study compared bright glasses with dim ones, not glasses with daylight.

The authors said the next test belongs with people whose schedules fight their body clocks.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Applied Psychology.

#123032. Industry News: People taking drugs like Ozempic report an unexpected change in their drinking habits

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1204 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: People taking drugs like Ozempic report an unexpected change in their drinking habits

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1204 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many people taking GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic reported drinking less alcohol within three months of starting their treatment.
  • People take Ozempic for many reasons, but cutting back on alcohol is rarely one of them.
  • adults examined changes in drinking habits after people started taking GLP-1 medications.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many people taking GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic reported drinking less alcohol within three months of starting their treatment.

People take Ozempic for many reasons, but cutting back on alcohol is rarely one of them. Yet some patients have noticed a change in their drinking habits after starting the medication.

A national survey of U.S. adults examined changes in drinking habits after people started taking GLP-1 medications.

Among those who drank alcohol before treatment, 44.2% reported drinking less within the first three months.

The change was even more common among people whose drinking habits put them at greater risk of health problems.

The research was led by Lori Uscher-Pines, a distinguished senior research scientist at the Brown University School of Public Health, along with colleagues from several other research institutions.

Recent findings suggest that ozempic and Wegovy contain semaglutide, a drug that helps regulate blood sugar and appetite. Both belong to a class of medicines called GLP-1 drugs.

Scientists are now exploring whether these medicines might also change how people respond to alcohol.

Early clinical trials have produced encouraging results. One possible explanation involves parts of the brain that control cravings and the sense of pleasure people get from certain activities.

Haiden Huskamp, the Henry J. Kaiser Professor of Health Care Policy at Harvard Medical School, is the study’s senior author.

“Because all of the evidence had been anecdotal when we started this study, it was hard to know what to expect,” said Huskamp.

“But finding that about half of GLP-1 users who drink reported reductions in their alcohol use after starting the medication is pretty striking.”.

In March and April 2026, the researchers surveyed members of the RAND American Life Panel, a group of randomly selected adults from across the United States.

Of the 2,857 people invited to participate, 2,009 completed the survey. Their average age was just under 49.

Recent findings suggest that among the respondents, 368 people had taken a GLP-1 drug at some point. Some were still taking the medication, while others had stopped.

The researchers asked these individuals to think back to their first three months of treatment and describe any changes in their drinking habits.

According to recent reports, not everyone who took these medications drank alcohol. After excluding 126 non-drinkers, the researchers were left with a group of 242 people.

Just over half, 52.6%, noticed no difference in their drinking habits. Another 44.2% said they drank less than before.

Only 3.3% reported an increase in alcohol consumption.

In other words, reports of drinking less were about 13 times as common as reports of drinking more.

The researchers were particularly interested in people whose drinking could put their health at risk.

They used a screening question developed by the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism.

Women were asked how often they had consumed four or more drinks on one occasion during the previous year, while the threshold for men was five drinks.

In a recent development, across the survey, 37.3% of adults reported at least one such occasion. Among GLP-1 users who met this criterion and drank alcohol, 54.1% reported drinking less after starting treatment.

Another 40.2% noticed no change, while 5.7% mentioned they drank more.

It has been revealed that age, income, sex, race, ethnicity and general health could all potentially influence a person’s relationship with alcohol. The researchers accounted for these factors in their analysis.

Even after doing so, people who screened positive for potentially unhealthy drinking had 2.3 times the odds of reporting a reduction in alcohol consumption.

None of the demographic factors showed a significant association with reporting less drinking.

The findings do not necessarily mean that the drugs work better for heavy drinkers. However, they give researchers a reason to study this particular group more closely.

It has been revealed that ask someone what Ozempic does, and they will probably mention weight loss. Far fewer people appear to know about its possible effects on drinking.

Nearly 80% of survey participants knew that GLP-1 drugs could help people lose weight, and 45.7% knew about their role in blood sugar control.

It has been revealed that yet only 9.7% had heard that these medicines might reduce the desire to drink alcohol. Awareness was somewhat higher among people with potentially unhealthy drinking habits.

According to recent reports, uscher-Pines expects public interest to grow as more research becomes available. Greater demand could also raise questions about insurance coverage and access to prescriptions through telehealth services.

Excessive alcohol consumption contributes to about 178,000 deaths in the United States every year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

For some people, drinking less is not simply a matter of deciding to stop. Alcohol use disorder is a medical condition that makes it difficult to control drinking, even when it causes serious problems.

Medications already exist to help people manage this condition. However, many of those who need help never receive it.

Alisa Busch, a professor of psychiatry at Harvard Medical School, was also involved in the study.

“The national surveys show that far and away most people with alcohol-use disorder receive no treatment, period,” said Busch.

There is a considerable difference between asking people whether they drink less and proving that a medication helps them do so.

“We weren’t testing GLP-1s for efficacy in reducing alcohol use. We’d need a randomized control trial for that,” Busch stated.

“We were trying to understand, in a population at higher risk for harmful drinking, is there a difference in their experience of drinking alcohol compared to individuals who screen negative.”.

Without a controlled experiment, the researchers cannot rule out other reasons for the changes in drinking habits.

People answered questions about something that had already happened. Their memories may not have been entirely accurate, and some participants may have given answers they thought were more socially acceptable.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers also don’t know how much less alcohol people consumed. Someone who skipped an occasional glass of wine and someone who stopped drinking altogether could both have reported a reduction.

Nor does the study tell us whether these changes lasted beyond the first three months of treatment.

Importantly, the screening question identified potentially unhealthy drinking habits rather than diagnosed cases of alcohol use disorder.

Researchers now need to find out whether GLP-1 drugs can produce meaningful and lasting reductions in alcohol consumption.

“If future studies lead to [Food and Drug Administration] approval of GLP-1s to treat alcohol use disorder, this could be a game changer in addiction treatment,” Uscher-Pines noted.

“Clinicians we spoke to are very excited about the potential here.”.

“The evidence isn’t there, but it will be very interesting to watch over the next couple of years,” Huskamp said. “There are trials underway. I don’t expect it to take too long before more evidence starts coming through.”.

In a recent development, for now, GLP-1 drugs are not approved for treating alcohol use disorder. But what patients have noticed while taking these medications may help scientists develop new ways to treat a condition that remains difficult to manage.

The study is published in the journal JAMA Psychiatry.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Stronger and more frequent severe weather events are making a compelling argument for investing in a home generator.
  • The term “home generator” can be confusing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Stronger and more frequent severe weather events are making a compelling argument for investing in a home generator. A large portable generator or a permanently installed standby generator can keep your entire home powered and operational for several days, or at least keep a few critical appliances such as a refrigerator running until the power comes back on. The cost of emergency power is never a small investment, though it is an increasingly notable one.

The term “home generator” can be confusing. It’s an unofficial category that includes larger portable generators capable of powering several appliances or a few critical circuits using a transfer switch (not all portable generators are built for this task). It also includes permanently installed standby generators that can automatically switch to whole-home backup power when the lights go out. Choosing the right size generator primarily comes down to how much power you think you’ll need in an emergency.

It has been revealed that there are many reliable home generators that deliver a great deal of power. Some offer you the choice of running on multiple different fuels, while other models use an inverter that can give you quieter and “cleaner” operation. There is a nice range of prices available, too, so you can easily find a generator below that fits your needs as well as your budget.

For the generators on this list that we tested, we considered the difficulty of unboxing, assembling, and starting each generator for the first time, because few things are as frustrating as buying a tool that turns out to be unnecessarily complicated from the get-go.

Once set up, the generators we reviewed were subjected to different load conditions, including things such as power tools, home appliances, and even recharging large power stations. We assessed the features that distinguish these generators from each other, including safety features, app connectivity, and portability, among other things.

A few picks on our list have not been tested, but we included them here after considerable research, taking into account the brand’s reputation, our knowledge of its product lines, various outside reviews, and our own experience testing similar models from those same brands.

Industry observers note that the DuroMax XP11000iH is a powerful midsize dual-fuel inverter generator, capable of keeping most homes up and running for an extended period of time. Inverter generators are a step above traditional generators because they convert alternating current (AC) to direct current (DC) and then back again to AC. This process creates cleaner, more efficient power and enables the generator to run more quietly and fuel efficiently.

Sources indicate that having two fuel options—gas and propane—provides a major boost of convenience by allowing you to use whatever’s handy. No gasoline? You can use the same tank of propane you use for your gas grill. It’s also parallel-capable, so you can daisy-chain it with another generator if you need extra power.

Industry observers note that the generator is enclosed in a large, sturdy plastic casing, which makes it durable and provides a fair amount of sound dampening. Of the many gas generators I’ve tested, it may be the quietest model that’s capable of backing up a whole home, especially when it’s running on propane, which trims it down by another few decibels. At 61 decibels on a 20 percent load, it’s about as loud as a dishwasher. Most comparably sized generators go up to around 80 decibels—about the same volume as a police siren.

Sources indicate that in addition to a full suite of essential modern safety features such as a carbon monoxide shutoff and low-oil shutoff, it goes the extra mile with lots of little touches, like remote start. The integrated battery tender keeps it ready to start, no matter how long it’s been sitting, which can be a lifesaver, too. When you do run out to check it, an onboard display reveals you key stats such as hours run, current load, and voltage output.

The only downside I could find was its weight. At upward of 200 pounds, it isn’t easy to carry. It does have wheels and sturdy handles, though, so it isn’t hard to wheel around on flat, paved ground—if you can push a loaded wheelbarrow, you can push this. Not that you’ll need to move it much; it’s a very sturdy generator, and it comes assembled with the wheels and handles attached (not all generators come with those pre-attached). —Reviewed by Nick Hilden.

Technically, there are cheaper generators out there, but the Generac GP9500E offers an outstanding blend of capability, quality, and durability at a very reasonable price. As such, this is where I’d steer you if you’re trying to shave down your spend.

Its 9,500-watt running capacity is slightly higher than the DuroMax’s, and it’s capable of powering all but the largest of homes. It can get a little noisy under a heavy load, but that’s common with units this size. It let out a relatively moderate purr when it was just powering the lights and a few appliances, but it became more of a roar when the heat kicked on.

With three fuel options—gas, propane, and natural gas—you get about as much versatility as you could possibly expect from a generator. A relatively large 7.5-gallon gas tank delivers a long runtime between fill-ups. And, while I was initially skeptical as to the necessity of the third fuel option, having natural gas support showed its value when a storm knocked out the power, and I didn’t have gas or propane on hand. All I needed to do was plug it into the natural gas line, and suddenly my house was the only one on the block with lights on.

According to recent reports, beyond that, though, it’s a fairly basic model. It has essential safety features such as low-oil and CO shutdown, but lacks elements such as a fancy digital display, remote start, or app. I don’t necessarily think that’s a problem: It can be helpful to get a piece of machinery that doesn’t go overboard with features. Its control panel is about as straightforward as can be, and it’s a cinch to get up and running.

Sources indicate that like my top pick, the GP9500E is exceedingly heavy. It’s also quite sturdy, though, which feels like a fair trade. The outlet covers aren’t as flimsy and breakable as with many other models of a similar price point. It isn’t completely immobile: It has wheels and handles that make it easy to cart around short distances. Realistically, though, weight is almost always going to be an concern with any generator capable of backing up your house.

Ultimately, its selling point is the price. It’s hard to find a quality tri-fuel generator for around $1,100, and the GP9500E performs well if you don’t mind losing out on some bells and whistles.

Industry observers note that whether you’re connecting devices individually, powering an RV, or running home backup power during a storm, this generator from Westinghouse (model WGen9500DF) covers all the bases. In addition to being dual-fuel (gas or propane), it includes both 30- and 50-amp outputs capable of powering 120- and 240-volt circuits. That means you could connect this generator to a transfer switch installed in your home using either option. And with 9,500 running watts of power, it’s enough for several critical circuits in your home, including the ones that run on 240 volts, such as a heating/ventilation/air-conditioning system, electric dryer, or well pump.

In a recent development, several other features caught our attention, including a push-button electric start and stop (no need to mess with a pull cable), plus a remote start key fob. There’s an automatic low-oil shutoff, and the display provides the voltage output, frequency, and lifetime hours (this can run up to 12 hours on a 6.6-gallon tank of gasoline). The only drawback is the 74-decibel noise level. While that’s typical of generators of this type, if you're planning on using this to power an RV or camper, it may be too loud for some parks, as many limit generator noise to under 70 decibels.

While it does not offer as much power as some of the choices on our list, Champion’s 4,750-watt generator has enough capacity to run three or four critical 120-volt circuits in your home during an outage. It will also power small to medium campers and RVs via a dedicated 30-amp, 120-volt RV receptacle. Listed at around $600, this generator gives you a lot for the price you pay.

Sources indicate that this generator uses a 224-cc engine with a 4.7-gallon fuel tank, enabling it to run for up to 14 hours (up to 10 hours using propane). A gauge displays a readout of the runtime hours and voltage output, and there’s an automated shutoff feature if the oil starts to run low. Since it’s dual-fuel, this generator can run off propane in addition to gasoline. For instance, if you are using it with an RV, you can run it off a camper’s propane tank without having to pack and haul a gas can. Likewise, with the included adapter hose, you can hook it up to a 20-pound propane tank.

There are a few drawbacks. Beyond the somewhat low wattage output for whole-home backup, there are no 240-volt outlets, so if you need that many volts to power circuits in your home for something such as a dryer or water heater, this model won’t be right for you. But if you just need something to keep some lights on and run a few appliances, this generator will get the job done and not cost you a ton of money up front to do it. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford.

There are many reasons to opt for an inverter generator, but the two biggest ones are: cleaner, more stable power (crucial for powering electronics safely) and less noise. Loudness becomes a major factor with larger generators, as more power requires a more powerful engine. That’s why we were so impressed with this model (EU7000iS) from Honda. It delivers a lot of power but at notably low loudness levels.

Sources indicate that it’s key to note that this is not a small generator. It weighs in at 263 pounds, making it one of the heaviest on our list. That mentioned, we found it fairly comfortable to move around. The metal frame that houses the generator has a folding handle that locks into place and is capped with soft grips, while on the front of the frame there are strong 10-inch rubber wheels. This made it fairly easy to roll around, even up some gradual slopes.

It’s also quite sturdy. The outer casing is constructed of stamped metal and impact-resistant composite hard plastic, with two large, hinged maintenance doors that lock into place.

It has been revealed that once we fired up the generator, it was noticeably quieter than other models we’ve tested, even when outputting a 60 percent load. Using an app-based sound meter, we were reading around 70 decibels from 15 feet away, which is lower than you would see with a non-inverter generator. This is helped by an “Eco Throttle” mode that adjusts the engine speed to meet demand as different devices are added, but we found even the standard throttle mode was fairly quiet as well.

Other things we liked were an app that allows for remote operation over Bluetooth, ground fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) protection, a carbon monoxide (CO) sensor, and 240-volt output over a 30-amp connection, which will let the generator connect to a manual transfer switch for sending direct power to your home electrical box.

Recent findings suggest that the two downsides are the cost (it’s very expensive at more than $4,000) and the fact that it can only be powered by gasoline; Honda doesn’t offer dual- or tri-fuel models for using propane or natural gas. But if those two considerations don’t bother you, the EU7000iS Inverter Generator is a high-quality machine that will keep you more quietly powered than some of the competition.

Full Honda EU7000iS 7000-Watt Inverter Generator Review.

It has been revealed that battery-based backup systems are getting smarter and more powerful every year, making them an increasingly strong contender to fuel-based standby generators. This model from EcoFlow is one of the most powerful we’ve tested.

The power station combines a separate inverter unit with two 6-kilowatt-hour batteries for a total of 12-kilowatt-hour capacity. That’s enough to run power-hungry devices simultaneously—things such as heating/ventilation/air-conditioning systems, electric ovens and dryers, microwaves, and air-conditioning units. Add to this increased solar input, and you can recharge faster, too. For our tests, we connected this to a home electrical system in the home using EcoFlow’s Smart Home Panel 3, which acts as the automatic transfer switch.

During testing, our reviewer experienced two power outages, one for a few seconds and one for several minutes. This power station features an Emergency Power Supply (EPS) mode, which facilitates a 20-millisecond switch to backup power—without this set, it normally switches in about five seconds. During the longer outage, the switch from grid to backup power, and then back again, was seamless. It was fast enough that the lights never flickered and the internet never dropped.

Several advanced smart features stand out. The smartphone app enables you to view power usage, down to the circuit, preset what circuits get backup power during outages, manually turn circuits on and off, and schedule automated tasks such as charging and discharging. You’ll also receive notifications when the grid goes down and the backup power takes over. If you live in an area where electricity is cheaper during low-peak hours, it can also prioritize recharging from grid power by choosing those times of day.

Meanwhile, this system is highly expandable. You can add up to eight more batteries for a total of 10, and an inlet box that comes with the smart panel has three ports. You could plug a Delta Pro Ultra X, bolstered by extra batteries, into each port to increase the total energy storage up to a whopping 184.3 kilowatt-hours of capacity and 36 kilowatts of continuous output.

Sources indicate that one of the biggest things our reviewer appreciates about the Delta Pro Ultra X and Smart Home Panel 3 is the peace of mind it gives. If the grid goes down, they know that their home systems will continue to run. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford.

Recent findings suggest that when AC power isn’t available, the greenest way to recharge a power station is with solar panels. However, the panel’s maximum power output often exceeds the maximum solar input, so they just can’t recharge fast enough. In these cases, whole-home, battery-based backup systems need the help of a fuel-based generator to recharge, so you’re not left high and dry if the power’s still out. That’s where the EcoFlow Smart Generator 4000 comes in.

This dual-fuel (gas or propane) generator connects to select EcoFlow power stations via a DC charging and communication cable, including the Delta Pro, Delta Pro 3, Delta 3, Delta 3 Plus, and Delta 2 Max. (Note: If your preferred brand is Anker, it also makes a fuel generator that’s compatible with some of its power stations, the 5500 Tri-Fuel Inverter Generator, which we also tested and reviewed.) This DC connection allows autonomous operation, so when a station’s battery hits critically low levels, the generator automatically starts to recharge it.

You can also recharge non-DC-compatible power stations by simply plugging them into the AC output, though it’s a slower recharge. If it’s an EcoFlow station, you can still automate startup, too, by pairing over Bluetooth. But you won’t be able to do this with other brands of power stations.

It has been revealed that our test editor Bradley Ford noted that EcoFlow’s app is one of the best features of this generator. Connecting over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, he used it to monitor fuel consumption and output, as well as set automated functions. He also tested how it can set the charging speed, monitor power output, and schedule times to start and stop the generator. He especially liked that the app provides a lot of useful information as well, such as generator fuel usage and estimated runtime.

In a recent development, of course, it can work as a standalone generator, too, though there are some limitations. Ford notes that there are only two outlets: a 120-volt, 20-amp outlet and a 120-volt, 30-amp outlet. The latter outlet can connect to a manual transfer switch installed in your home, but it won’t be able to power any 240-volt circuits, and the total output of 3,200 watts is only enough to power a few circuits. However, he thinks it would work well for RV use, and because it’s an inverter generator, it’s better at safely powering sensitive electronics like TVs and computers. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford.

Full EcoFlow Dual-Fuel Smart Generator 4000 Review.

According to recent reports, pulsar is a relatively upcoming brand in the generator business and doesn’t have a long track record. We first spotted it on Amazon and didn’t seriously consider its generators for testing. That was, up until our test editor needed a generator (with specific features and on a budget) after a generator failed at his solar-powered off-grid cabin. Happily, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel Inverter Generator highlighted up quickly and didn’t disappoint.

The generator was easy to assemble and prep, taking only 15 minutes. After adding oil, it was connected to a propane cylinder and was up and running on the first cycle of the starter. Our first task was to charge a solar battery bank during a wintertime period when there was not enough available sunlight, and it worked perfectly.

In a recent development, we have logged more than 20 hours of use so far, running it primarily on propane connected to a 100-pound cylinder (enough fuel to last a couple of months). This Pulsar puts out very clean power, with a claimed total harmonic distortion (THD) of less than 3 percent, which met the requirements of the solar inverter-charger I was using. Using the inverter to monitor the current frequency, we found that it was indeed very stable with minimal variance, between 59.97 and 60.09 Hz. All things considered, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel is a good value for the specs, capacity, and features. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford.

True whole-home backup requires a professionally installed standby generator like Generac’s 22-kilowatt home standby generator. It’s designed to power a house that’s roughly 2,500 square feet. If you need to run specialized medical devices, work from home, or have kids who are learning from home, this model is a sound investment.

Sources indicate that another benefit of this bundle is that it includes a transfer switch, which is required if you’re planning to install this type of generator. It supports 200-amp electrical service, providing the backup circuits needed to power high-voltage appliances such as refrigerators and well pumps, along with air conditioning and heating systems. Plus, there’s built-in WiFi for checking the status of your generator and receiving maintenance alerts when you’re not at home.

Industry observers note that you could just drive over to your local hardware store and buy a large portable generator to use as a home backup, but we wouldn’t recommend it. You want to make sure you’re getting a generator that can back up your home and power all the appliances, lights, and electronics inside. (Plus some extra watts in case you need them down the line.).

Sources indicate that in addition, there are often state and local laws or homeowners association rules and restrictions around using them in residential neighborhoods. Choosing poorly or setting up your backup generator incorrectly could damage the generator or short out your house power at best, or lead to fire, electrocution, or carbon monoxide poisoning at worst.

According to recent reports, picking the best generator for your home starts with a little math. Ideally, you want to calculate how much energy you need to keep your house running, and buy a generator that can handle everything you want to power in an emergency, with room to spare.

The two key specs to pay attention to are the running wattage and starting wattage (e.g., 9,500 running watts / 12,500 starting watts). Running wattage is effectively your generator’s capacity: It tells you how much power a generator can produce steadily without any possibility of an overload. Starting wattage is the generator’s max output, or how much power it can produce for short, peak bursts when appliances first switch on.

In a recent development, when you are making your list, note what items are 120-volt and which ones are 240-volt appliances. It’s not hard to identify them. Refrigerators, small appliances, and most electronics run on 120-volt power and plug into standard outlets. Anything that requires 240 volts—electric dryers, well pumps, and HVAC systems—is either hardwired into your electrical system or has a dedicated 240-volt outlet. If you need to power the latter, the installation of a transfer switch and a generator that outputs at least 30 amps/240 volts may be required.

If you’re just looking to keep the fridge, lights, and a few modest appliances going through a short blackout, you can usually get away with a generator that supplies 3,000 to 5,000 watts. If you want to run the heat, hot water, and several appliances at once, blueprint on using at least 6,000 to 8,000 watts. If you think you’re going to be adding large appliances such as laundry machines and dishwashers, expect to need 10,000 watts or more.

According to recent reports, A piece of advice we have: Once you figure out how much you need, opt for buying a generator that outputs around 20 percent more than that. It’s not uncommon to realize you need more than you thought you would.

Recent findings suggest that it’s also important to consider that, while generators are certainly a hefty investment, they usually stand the test of time. Consumer-grade portable generators can run anywhere from 1,000 to 3,000 hours, sometimes more. If you run one for 100 hours per year, it should last for 10 to 30 years.

There are four basic types of generators, each with advantages and disadvantages.

The most traditional of the generator category, these run on carbon-based fuels like gasoline, propane, and natural gas. Some allow you to switch between them. Dual-fuel models add the option of either propane or natural gas, while tri-fuel versions offer all three fuel options. These generators can be small, offering as little as 1,000 watts of power output, or run very large, as much as 20,000 watts or more.

Different fuels offer different power capabilities. For example, a tri-fuel generator may offer 9,500 running watts and 12,500 starting watts with gasoline, but only 8,500/11,200 with propane and 7,500/9,500 with natural gas. Regardless of the fuel you choose, this type of generator must always be operated 5 to 20 feet away from the home or any window or door, because the carbon monoxide exhaust is deadly. Even a garage with an open door is not safe.

Recent findings suggest that often this type of generator is called portable, but that's a relative term: Almost all of them weigh more than 100 pounds, and many are upwards of 200. Many are on wheels, making them relatively easy to store in a garage and wheel outside when you need them, but actually moving one will likely require at least two people.

Inverter generators look and operate the same as other portable generators, but have an added component–a power inverter– that converts the alternating current (AC) power generated by its fuel source to DC (Direct Current), then inverts it back to AC before putting it out.

It has been revealed that generators without an inverter generate varying degrees of distortion in the sine wave of the alternating current, which can trigger power surges and other complications in some electronics. The inverter stabilizes the power, almost like a filter, “cleaning” it for more sensitive electronics like TVs and laptops.

So why doesn’t every generator have an inverter? Inverters are expensive, so the generators are, too.

Realistically speaking, you don’t need an inverter generator to power major appliances and your house power, but if you’re running a full home backup (or if you count a TV or laptop among your essential electronics), holding out for an inverter is a smart move.

It has been revealed that while often referred to as “solar generators” because they can be paired with solar panels, power stations are not really true generators. They're advanced battery banks that store power, which you precharge using AC power or solar panels. They can’t generate electricity in real time.

But because they can offer many of the same electrical outputs as a fuel generator, they can function similarly to a traditional generator for as long as the batteries retain a charge. Some stations are very small and meant only for off-grid adventures like camping trips, but some are large enough to run whole-home systems that can produce 14,400 watts or more with expandable batteries.

Since power stations don't run on fuel or have an engine, they can be used indoors without the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning and operate with almost no noise.

The downside is that once the power is depleted, the power station must be recharged. If the power grid is still unavailable, it can take many hours in ideal sunny conditions if all you have are solar panels. You can use a traditional generator to recharge a power station, but some may view that as defeating the purpose.

Standby generators are permanently installed generators designed to automatically take over for your house power in the event of an outage. You can set them to power your whole house, or only specific circuits, giving you precise control. Standby generators start at around 10,000 watts (10 kilowatts) but can go up to much higher. For the average home, a range of 10 to 25 kilowatts is usually enough.

In a recent development, they typically require professional installation, making them the most costly option. Since many large portable generators can effectively back up a house for a few hours for a lot less money, standby models are still considered a more niche option.

In a recent development, when you draw too much power from your generator, its performance will start to decline. At home, your lights will start to dim or flicker, and appliances may turn off momentarily. The generator itself may also start to get louder, or sound like it’s working extra hard to keep up.

If you notice these signs, start turning off and unplugging non-essential power sources immediately, or turn the generator off entirely for ten minutes or so to reduce the power load.

In a recent development, this is an urgent problem, so do not wait to take action: If you overwork your generator for too long, it’s only a matter of time before it starts to overheat, produce smoke, or break down. The damage from an extended overload could permanently damage the generator or, worse, start a fire.

Recent findings suggest that with the right size for your home, a portable or standby generator can run as long as you keep feeding it fuel and stay within its running wattage capacity; however, you should not run them indefinitely. Manufacturers recommend you allow them to rest for 30 minutes or more after at least 24 hours of use. Check the manual of your generator for its specific recommendations.

You will get more time from each tank of gas if you draw less power, so it helps to pay extra attention to your electricity usage when you’re running the generator.

Make sure to turn your gas and/or propane generators off when it’s time to refill the tank. Failing to do so could lead to a fire.

Power stations, since they rely on electricity or solar power, can almost always be charged while in use.

It has been revealed that never run a fuel-based generator (gasoline, propane, natural gas) indoors. Burning fuel releases carbon monoxide (CO), which will quickly build up to deadly levels in an enclosed space.

Set your generator up outside, between 5 and 20 feet away from your home and/or any garages, sheds, or other walls. Position it as far as possible from doors, windows, and vents, with the exhaust positioned away from the house, to minimize the possibility of fumes wafting in. If you keep it outside all year round, find a naturally covered position where snow won’t naturally pile up around it.

Industry observers note that my generator is situated near my home’s power box, which is located on a windowless side of my home. It stands about five feet from the exterior wall, with plenty of space on all sides, but close enough to sit under the roof peak overhang 20 feet above.

According to recent reports, david is a Reviews Editor for Hearst’s Enthusiast Group, contributing to Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, Best Products, and Biography. He has over 25 years of experience writing about and reviewing consumer electronics, kitchen appliances, DIY products, outdoor gear, and more. He also spent years covering the ever-changing world of online retail. To relax, he loves experimenting with latest recipes, tweaking his smart home setup, and spending time outdoors on his bike or camping.

Pakistan’s first astronaut heads for China’s space station

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (902 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 24, Roscosmos is targeting 5:13 a.m.
  • EST, Arianespace will try again to launch an Ariane 64 from the Guiana Space Centre in French Guiana with 36 Amazon Leo satellites.
  • According to recent reports, later that morning, at 10:55 a.m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Tuesday, Nov. 24, Roscosmos is targeting 5:13 a.m. EST to launch the Progress MS-36 cargo ship to the International Space Station (ISS) on a Soyuz-2.1b from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan, according to Next Spaceflight. NASA still lists the flight only as no earlier than fall 2026 and has not given a date.

Sources indicate that at 5:45 a.m. EST, Arianespace will try again to launch an Ariane 64 from the Guiana Space Centre in French Guiana with 36 Amazon Leo satellites. A problem with the rocket’s ground support systems halted Monday’s countdown. It is Amazon’s first launch since last week’s Vulcan failure.

According to recent reports, later that morning, at 10:55 a.m. EST, SpaceX will launch the classified USSF-266 mission for the U.S. Space Force from Space Launch Complex 4E (SLC-4E) at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. Neither SpaceX nor the Space Force has stated what the rocket carries. The booster will land on the droneship Of Course I Still Love You in the Pacific Ocean.

That evening, at 7:18 p.m. EST, a Long March 2F is slated to launch Shenzhou-24, carrying three astronauts, from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China to the Tiangong space station, per Next Spaceflight.

Sources indicate that one seat makes history. A Pakistani astronaut will fly as a payload specialist, becoming the first foreign visitor to Tiangong and Pakistan’s first astronaut. Pakistan’s space agency, the Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (SUPARCO), has shortlisted two pilots, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud. One will fly and the other will serve as backup. The astronaut is expected to spend about a week on Tiangong and return to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft.

In a recent development, on Thursday, Nov. 26, the state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC) is targeting 4:35 a.m. EST for a Long March 2D launch from the Xichang Satellite Launch Center in southwestern China, according to Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been confirmed.

In a recent development, later Thursday, at 7:05 p.m. EST, Rocket Lab will launch Night Owls Never Sleep on an Electron from Launch Complex 1 on Upcoming Zealand’s Māhia Peninsula.The payload is a StriX satellite for the Japanese tech giant Synspective. StriX satellites use synthetic aperture radar to image the ground through clouds and darkness.

On Friday, Nov. 27, CASC is targeting 8:00 a.m. EST for a Long March 6A launch from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center in Shanxi province, according to Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been declared.

On Saturday, Nov. 28, CAS Space, a commercial launch organization backed by the Chinese Academy of Sciences, intends to launch a Kinetica 1 at 8:00 p.m. EST from a sea platform in the South China Sea, supported by the Haiyang Oriental Spaceport, per Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been announced.

Later Saturday, at 10:50 p.m. EST, a Long March 6C is slated to lift off from Taiyuan, according to Next Spaceflight. Its payload is also undisclosed.

Finally, at 11:39 p.m. EST on Saturday, SpaceX returns to SLC-4E for USSF-380, another classified Space Force mission. The booster is again slated to land on Of Course I Still Love You.

It has been revealed that closing out the week on Sunday, Nov. 29, NASA and Northrop Grumman are targeting 10:47 a.m. EST to launch the NG-25 Cygnus XL cargo spacecraft on a Falcon 9 from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. Named the S.S. James A. Lovell after the late Apollo 13 commander, the spacecraft will haul several tons of science and supplies to the ISS.

In a recent development, last week opened on Wednesday, Nov. 18, at 5:51 p.m. EST, when a Long March 2D lifted off from Taiyuan carrying Shijian-24. China has not remarked what the satellite does; CGTN reported only that it reached its planned orbit.

On Friday, Nov. 20, at 6:59 a.m. EST, a Long March 8A debuted from the commercial launch site at Wenchang with the 30th batch of satellites for Guowang, China’s state-backed broadband megaconstellation.

According to recent reports, that night, at 11:20 p.m. EST, SpaceX debuted the classified USSF-317 mission from Vandenberg, two days later than planned. The booster landed on Of Course I Still Love You.

The week closed on Sunday, Nov. 22, at 7:23 a.m. EST, when a Falcon 9 lifted off from the same pad with the National Reconnaissance Office’s NROL-136, a day later than planned. The launch came 32 hours after USSF-317, SpaceX’s fastest turnaround between debuts from the same pad. The booster flew back to Landing Zone 4.

Sources indicate that south Korea’s Agency for Defense Development (ADD), the military research arm of its defense ministry, is still preparing the first full demonstration flight of its solid-fueled Mir rocket from an offshore platform near Jeju Island. After canceling a June 30 attempt over safety concerns, the ministry has noted only that it aims to launch by the end of the year.

ExPace, a subsidiary of the state-owned China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation (CASIC), also has a Kuaizhou 11 launch from Jiuquan on the books no earlier than November 2026. Its payload has not been announced.

Brooks Mendenhall is a staff writer at Astronomy, based in Chattanooga, Tennessee, fueled by an unending curiosity about the universe. A former classroom teacher, he has a knack for breaking down complex concepts for a wide audience.

Van Hollen introduces bid for majority leader, but Schumer states he has the votes

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., left, has revealed a challenge to current Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y.
  • Chris Van Hollen confirmed Thursday night that he would run for Senate majority leader, launching a challenge to Sen.
  • Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat first elected to the Senate in 2016, served in leadership in the House and has been chairman of both the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., left, has revealed a challenge to current Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

Sen. Chris Van Hollen confirmed Thursday night that he would run for Senate majority leader, launching a challenge to Sen. Charles E. Schumer of Fresh York, the current Democratic leader.

Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat first elected to the Senate in 2016, served in leadership in the House and has been chairman of both the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. He has stated since the midterm elections he was listening to fellow Senate Democrats about the possibility of a run for the top job.

Sources indicate that “In this election, the American people called for change. They called for a change from Donald Trump’s disastrous policies but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn’t working for working people,” Van Hollen stated in a statement. “It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need upcoming leadership. This is not about any one person – it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.”.

Schumer has already remarked he has the votes needed to continue serving as the leader.

“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead. I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader. I look forward to leading our newly introduced Democratic majority and delivering for the American people,” Schumer said in a statement.

It has been revealed that schumer's supporters were quick to highlight the success at the ballot box in 2026, with the Democratic caucus potentially growing to 56 seats if former Rep. Mary Peltola prevails in Alaska.

It has been revealed that “Chuck has outlined an aggressive blueprint for the newly introduced Democratic majority which is directly responsive to the message we heard from the voters, and he has the experience and unique mastery of the Senate process to make it happen,” Sen. Angus King, a Maine independent who caucuses with the Democrats, said in a statement. “Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?”.

In a recent development, in keeping with the World Series theme, Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., echoed King with her own statement of support for Schumer.

“The Brewers just had a record season, and next year is not the time to change our management," Baldwin said. "The same is true in the Senate.”.

In an interview with MS NOW about his run, Van Hollen conceded that Schumer would be the favorite in the secret-ballot contest, which will take place in December.

It has been revealed that “Am I the underdog? Yes,” Van Hollen said. “You’re talking about an incumbent who uses the power of incumbency to, you know, provide deals to people.”.

In a recent development, van Hollen outlined legislative priorities including restoring Medicaid funding that Republicans cut in last year's budget reconciliation law and extending Affordable Care Act tax credits. But he suggested Democrats need to go further.

"We need to extend tax credits for the Affordable Care Act, but we can’t stop there, right? We have a completely broken health care system. It’s become profits, not people. And so my view is, we also need in the first 100 days to make health care more affordable for tens of millions of people," Van Hollen remarked. "We need to immediately make it clear that nobody’s going to pay one penny to subsidize data centers. ... We need to make sure that we have a livable minimum wage.".

He also stated he would not take sides in contested Democratic primaries, and he would make sure the DSCC did not take money from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC.

Van Hollen's early backers include progressive Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who emerged from a hotly contested Democratic primary in Michigan while the Senate Democratic political apparatus was backing Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich.

According to recent reports, “In April, I was the first candidate in the country to call on Senator Chris Van Hollen to lead Senate Democrats, and I am proud to stand with him in his bid to become Senate Majority Leader,” El-Sayed said in a statement. “Michiganders demand money out of politics, money in pockets, and Medicare for All. Sen. Chris Van Hollen offers both the courage to go toe-to-toe with the Trump administration to deliver for working people and the experience to maneuver the Senate caucus. It’s why he has my full support to lead our caucus.”.

Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

A golden bar of stars cuts through the heart of a spiral galaxy

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hubble’s portrait of NGC 4394 highlights how a bar of stars fits into a spiral galaxy and offers a rare perspective on the structure of our own Milky Way.
  • Today’s Image of the Day features a nearly face-on view of the spiral galaxy NGC 4394.
  • A pale gold bar stretches across the galaxy’s bright core, while thin lanes of dust curve around the center.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hubble’s portrait of NGC 4394 highlights how a bar of stars fits into a spiral galaxy and offers a rare perspective on the structure of our own Milky Way.

Today’s Image of the Day features a nearly face-on view of the spiral galaxy NGC 4394.

A pale gold bar stretches across the galaxy’s bright core, while thin lanes of dust curve around the center. Farther out, two spiral arms sweep into the dark.

That angle makes the bar easy to spot and gives us something we can only imagine for our own Milky Way: a view down onto the disk, with the center and the spiral arms visible in the same frame.

The European Space Agency released this Hubble Space Telescope image on November 24.

In a recent development, the galaxy lies about 55 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices. Its light was already on its way here long before humans appeared on Earth.

Industry observers note that on a clear, dark night, the Milky Way looks like a hazy band across the sky. That band is part of our galaxy’s disk seen from within.

When we look along the disk, stars at many different distances crowd into the same field of view, and dust obscures much of the light coming from the center.

Astronomers have used infrared telescopes such as Spitzer to look through some of that dust and trace the distribution of stars.

Industry observers note that those observations helped establish that our galaxy has a central bar. A face-on view of NGC 4394 makes it easier to picture how such a feature fits into a spiral galaxy.

According to recent reports, the angle also makes it easier to follow the dust. In Hubble’s image, narrow dark filaments arc around the core and wind through the disk.

They stand out where they block light from the stars behind them. Farther along the arms, blue and pink knots punctuate the softer glow of the surrounding stars.

A bar may look like a solid feature in a still image, but the stars that make it up are moving around the galaxy.

One way a bar can form is when nearly circular stellar orbits become stretched. If enough of those elongated orbits line up, the combined light from the stars takes on the shape of a bar.

Recent findings suggest that A passing galaxy can disturb a disk through gravity and help set that process in motion. A disk can also become unstable through gravitational interactions among its own stars.

Either way, a feature that spans a large part of the galaxy can emerge from changes in the paths of individual stars.

Once a bar forms, its gravity can help channel gas inward. That matters because gas supplies the raw material for fresh stars.

A bar can therefore influence where a galaxy builds its next generation of stars, even though the bright feature we see in the image is mostly the light of stars already there.

According to recent reports, hubble first captured NGC 4394 while studying a different galaxy. One instrument was trained on nearby Messier 85 and its star clusters, while another recorded an adjacent patch of sky containing NGC 4394.

Hubble’s team released that earlier image about a decade ago.

Sources indicate that the newly introduced portrait combines those observations with data from a program studying 40 galaxies. NGC 4394 belongs to the Virgo Cluster, a gathering of more than 1,000 galaxies.

The researchers want to understand how star formation winds down in crowded environments and whether it follows a different course in galaxies with fewer neighbors.

Sources indicate that star clusters give researchers a way to look backward. By comparing how brightly a cluster shines at different wavelengths, astronomers can estimate its age.

According to recent reports, A young cluster marks a place where stars formed relatively recently. Older clusters preserve evidence of earlier activity.

Taken together, their ages and locations can help researchers reconstruct where star formation persisted and where it faded.

In a recent development, that gives the specks along the spiral arms a second role in the image. The bar is the feature you can pick out at a glance, and it offers an immediate point of comparison with the Milky Way.

Recent findings suggest that the star clusters are harder to spot. Each one carries a piece of the galaxy’s history, and Hubble can pick them out even though their light has crossed 55 million years of space to reach us.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

In an increasingly fire-prone western North America, Jennifer Grenz, an ecologist and member of the Lytton First Nation, looks at fire with a holistic eye. She considers her work with landscapes recovering from catastrophic wildfire to be “deliberately unfocused,” spanning soil microbial ecology, restoration ecology, invasion biology and historical biology.

Recent findings suggest that grenz analyzes historical ecological records, like how Indigenous people have shaped and cared for ecosystems over time, to paint a comprehensive picture. “I’m interested in how those histories leave ecological legacies and hints of the stewardship of the past,” notes Grenz, who leads the Indigenous Ecology Lab at the University of British Columbia in Canada. “What changed on the land that made it more vulnerable?”.

Grenz spends time with many kinds of specialists, such as archaeologists, anthropologists and Indigenous elders who provide oral histories.

Industry observers note that moving forward, her lab will examine ecology below ground, including soil, microbial communities and root networks. The goal is to understand the role of underground ecology in critical topics like carbon sequestration, climate change, biodiversity and sustainable management.

It has been revealed that “My motivation is in our interior Salish Territories in the southern interior of British Columbia, where my ancestors rest and where my people are,” Grenz says. “The responsibility I feel to them and to our Tmícw, which means our lands, [is] to not take us back to the past, but to show that we have the deep knowledge to help us move forward.”.
