Nov. 24, 1990: Keck I sees first light

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (186 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in 1985, the W.M.
  • 24, 1990, with only nine of the 36 segments of its mirror in place, Keck I turned skyward and achieved first light.
  • Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

It has been revealed that in 1985, the W.M. Keck Foundation donated $70 million for the University of California and Caltech to construct a upcoming observatory on Maunakea in Hawaii. The twin telescopes of the Keck Observatory would be larger than any previous telescope, and the first to use a segmented-mirror design. The goal was a facility that could see farther out into the universe, and with more detail, to study exoplanets, black holes, star and planet formation, and more.

On Nov. 24, 1990, with only nine of the 36 segments of its mirror in place, Keck I turned skyward and achieved first light. The telescope’s image of NGC 1232 was an auspicious beginning of a long career for the Keck Observatory, furthered when Keck I was completed in 1992, and when Keck II was constructed and saw first light in October 1996. The twin telescopes would become the most scientifically productive optical and infrared telescopes in the world.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

A group of visitors walks past the Capitol on Sept. 22. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo).

With stopgap funding set to expire in less than a month, Senate Republican appropriators Thursday unveiled a roughly $5.3 billion draft fiscal 2027 Legislative Branch spending bill that would boost security funding and sidestep contentious debates over a key watchdog.

The proposal would provide $965 million for Capitol Police, a nearly $83 million hike from fiscal 2026, but still short of the more than $1 billion the department requested as threats against lawmakers rise.

And it would bump funding for the Government Accountability Office up to $860 million, an increase of nearly 6 percent from fiscal 2026. That stands in contrast to the version of the bill advanced by the House Appropriations Committee in May, which floated slashing the GAO by 25 percent.

It joins several other draft spending bills released this week by Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, who is trying to kickstart bicameral negotiations as lawmakers stare down a Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government.

According to recent reports, her committee ran into a stalemate on topline numbers earlier this year that stopped it from marking up any of the 12 annual bills, but lawmakers nipped the threat of a government shutdown in the bud ahead of the midterm elections by pushing through a continuing resolution. With that funding now set to expire next month, appropriators are hoping they can wrap up at least some of the bills while punting the rest into the next Congress with another stopgap.

According to recent reports, the Legislative Branch bill is the smallest of the 12 appropriations bills and typically among the least controversial. But debates over the GAO have become a sticking point during the Trump administration as the agency accuses the White House of violating budget laws — a move the Office of Management and Budget has pushed back on, arguing the GAO has no authority over the administration since it is part of the legislative branch.

The GAO has been without a permanent head after its longtime leader Gene L. Dodaro retired last year, although Republicans are now making a last-ditch effort to get one confirmed during the lame-duck session before Democrats take power.

It has been revealed that the House version of the spending bill sought to bar the comptroller general from suing under the 1974 budget law restricting presidential impoundments, unless specifically authorized by Congress. But the Senate proposal includes no such language, and overall, it appears designed to avoid drastic or contentious moves.

It would also leave in place a provision that would block cost-of-living adjustments for members of Congress, whose pay has been frozen since 2009.

Senate Democrats, however, criticized the bill text after its release, saying it wouldn’t invest enough in the legislative branch.

“The Legislative Branch bill underfunds key work to support oversight of the Executive Branch, and it underfunds important efforts to keep the Capitol complex safe,” Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., mentioned in a statement.

The Architect of the Capitol would get $762.5 million, though funding for House office buildings is not included in that total. The agency is requesting $1.6 billion as it seeks to begin large-scale renovations of the Rayburn House Office Building. The architect has repeatedly warned lawmakers that parts of the Capitol complex are in need of critical infrastructure upgrades, arguing that delaying renovations will only make them more expensive as things continue to deteriorate.

The bill’s $5.3 billion proposal represents funding for the Senate and legislative branch agencies, while excluding House-only funds, which are typically added later.

In a recent development, isabel Angelo spends her days searching the cosmos for exoplanets and signs of extraterrestrial intelligence. But Angelo’s head isn’t in the stars. It’s buried under mountains of 0s and 1s — data from space telescopes old and upcoming.

To piece together a fuller picture of what’s out there (alien megastructures around nearby stars, perhaps?), Angelo and her colleagues at the SETI Institute in Mountain View, Calif., are turning to machine learning models. These tools are analyzing the troves of telescope data for anomalies — things that look “weird” in space that we don’t know how to explain yet.

Most of the space weirdos will probably turn out to be total normies — a comet, a newborn star or a star surrounded by lots of gas and dust. “These are things that I would expect [the models] to find,” Angelo says. “But the goal is to find something that’s not even in any of these categories.”.

In the meantime, Angelo keeps her whimsy and wonder for space alive by remembering historic moments, like the reveal of the first portrait of a black hole in 2019. The scientists “put all of these telescopes all over the Earth. They wait for the Earth to rotate. They do all this math to construct this one image,” Angelo says. “I can’t believe how creative and innovative we have to be to learn about space. It’s such a specific and really fun challenge.”.

Big hope and lots of help for a tiny fish that lives in a desert cave

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (868 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The endangered Devils Hole pupfish rebounded to 137 fish in October 2026, following captive-bred releases and feeding after earthquake damage.
  • Biologists counted 137 Devils Hole pupfish on Oct.
  • The fall 2025 survey had found 69 fish, and the spring 2026 survey found 77, according to the National Park Service (NPS).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The endangered Devils Hole pupfish rebounded to 137 fish in October 2026, following captive-bred releases and feeding after earthquake damage.

Biologists counted 137 Devils Hole pupfish on Oct. 10, 2026, in the only place the species lives in the wild: a water-filled cavern in the Nevada desert.

The fall 2025 survey had found 69 fish, and the spring 2026 survey found 77, according to the National Park Service (NPS).

Devils Hole is a detached unit of Death Valley National Park. It opens onto an aquifer, and Ash Meadows is the discharge point for a groundwater system that reaches more than 100 miles (160 kilometers) to the northeast.

According to recent reports, the cavern is more than 500 feet (152 meters) deep, and its bottom has never been mapped, according to the park’s Devils Hole page. The water stays at 92°F (33°C).

The fish forage and spawn on a shallow rock shelf near the surface, where they feed on algae and diatoms. That shelf, the population’s main feeding and breeding ground, covers about 215 square feet (20 square meters).

Industry observers note that the fish are about 1 to 1.5 inches (2.5 to 3.8 centimeters) long. Males are iridescent blue, while females are olive-green.

Recent findings suggest that the species has been isolated for 10,000 to 20,000 years, longer than any other pupfish in the Death Valley system. A presidential proclamation added Devils Hole to what was then Death Valley National Monument in 1952.

Scuba divers and surface counters from the NPS and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) survey the fish at the same time. Divers count in the cavern’s depths, while others watch the limestone shelf.

In a recent development, biologists have used these methods nearly every spring and fall since 1972. Through the mid-1990s, counts averaged about 200 fish in spring and 425 in fall.

In the early 2000s, spring counts averaged about 90. The number dropped to 35 in spring 2013.

Pupfish numbers naturally rise and fall. The two agencies say continued monitoring, research and habitat management remain essential.

Two earthquakes, one in December and the other in February, set off waves in the cavern’s normally still water. The waves moved algae, organic material and fish eggs off the shelf.

It has been revealed that A dive in March 2025 found only 20 or so fish. The official spring 2025 count recorded 38, down from 191 one year earlier.

“The present size at near-record lows deserves our serious attention, and the actions in the strategic initiative, including supplemental feeding and population augmentation, provide the best opportunity for recovery,” Michael Schwemm, a senior fish biologist with the USFWS, mentioned in April 2025.

“I’m proud of the work of this interagency team to monitor and protect the Devils Hole pupfish,” Mike Reynolds, superintendent of Death Valley National Park, said at the time.

An earthquake struck Panama, nearly 3,000 miles (4,800 kilometers) away, on Oct. 9, 2026, the day before the survey. Biologists first saw signs of stress in the fish, but a later visit found them in healthier condition.

According to recent reports, backup fish live at the Ash Meadows Fish Conservation Facility, built in 2013 with a Southern Nevada Public Land Management Act grant. Its refuge tank holds about 100,000 gallons (380,000 liters) and includes a replica of the Devils Hole habitat.

Industry observers note that staff collect eggs, aquatic invertebrates and algae from Devils Hole each month with NPS partners. They raise the young fish and add them to the refuge tank as young adults.

Industry observers note that in spring 2025, biologists added captive-raised fish to the wild population for the first time. In all, 72 such fish were released into Devils Hole between March 2025 and February 2026.

Teams also fed the wild fish while the algae recovered, using data from the facility and from NPS monitoring.

Recent findings suggest that “We were fortunate we had a strategic proposal that allowed us to act cautiously but swiftly,” remarked Kevin Wilson, an aquatic ecologist and Devils Hole program manager at Death Valley National Park, in May 2026. That plan guided the step of “moving the refuge tank fish to Devils Hole to assist with recovery,” he said.

Schwemm said the 2022 proposal “was instrumental in ensuring the wild population’s survival.”.

The rebound followed those releases of captive-raised fish and the months of supplemental feeding in Devils Hole.

It has been revealed that still, the pupfish lives only 10 to 14 months on average. Biologists therefore believe most of the fish in the October count hatched and grew up in Devils Hole.

“It’s exciting to see Devils Hole pupfish numbers increase so significantly over the past year,” Reynolds said this fall.

“While challenges remain, we’re encouraged by this progress and committed to its long-term survival,” he added.

Sources indicate that the species was listed as endangered in 1967. A 1976 court ruling in Cappaert v. United States recognized a water right for Devils Hole, and an injunction limited groundwater pumping to keep the shelf underwater.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service.

#123004. Astronomers catch ‘galaxy-killing’ wind in the act

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1390 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Astronomy ↗ Open Full Page

Astronomers catch ‘galaxy-killing’ wind in the act

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1390 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in the local universe, it is common to find galaxies that have stopped forming new stars.
  • Sources indicate that but ever since it first began surveying the cosmos, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has discovered more quiescent galaxies within the cosmos’ first 2 billion years than current models of galaxy formation and evolution predict.
  • Now, a team has found evidence that when galaxies collide — as they frequently did in the early universe — it can trigger a burst of star formation so intense that it generates winds capable of snuffing out the opportunity for any further stars to be born.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in the local universe, it is common to find galaxies that have stopped forming new stars. These so-called quiescent galaxies have lived for billions of years and over that time, gradually exhausted their star-forming gas. By contrast, galaxies that lie at much greater distances — and thus appear to us when they were young, in the early universe — should have plenty of gas and be readily forming stars.

Sources indicate that but ever since it first began surveying the cosmos, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has discovered more quiescent galaxies within the cosmos’ first 2 billion years than current models of galaxy formation and evolution predict. Astronomers don’t know why they have stopped forming stars so soon, but they have many theories. Some of them require dark energy to have had a stronger influence in the early universe than previously thought, and thus have profound impacts on our understanding of the universe and its evolution.

Now, a team has found evidence that when galaxies collide — as they frequently did in the early universe — it can trigger a burst of star formation so intense that it generates winds capable of snuffing out the opportunity for any further stars to be born. This could explain the high number of young but unexpectedly quiescent galaxies JWST has found without needing drastic changes to our understanding of dark energy and its influence over time.

According to recent reports, in order to form stars, galaxies need reservoirs of gas that are dense and cold, lacking energy and prone to collapsing inward. One way to end a galaxy’s era of star formation — a process that astronomers call quenching — is to trigger strong winds that blast outward from the galaxy. These vast, high-speed flows of charged particles can blow away or heat this cold gas.

Such galactic winds can have two possible sources of energy. One is an actively accreting central supermassive black hole (called an active galactic nucleus, or AGN). The other is the energetic blasts generated by massive stars that form and then quickly die, ending their lives by exploding as supernovae. But astronomers have never caught such a wind in the act of draining its host of gas in the early universe, as it is difficult to get a detailed look inside a galaxy so far away.

To better discern the inner workings of star-forming galaxies in the early universe, researchers carried out a joint survey combining observations taken with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) — a powerful radio observatory in Chile — and infrared data from JWST. They also turned to archival data from the Hubble Space Telescope. A team led by astrophysicist Rebecca Davies of Swinburne University of Technology in Australia spotted one particular galaxy, called CRISTAL-02, that shows what appears to be the first direct evidence of a wind powerful enough to halt star formation in a massive galaxy just 1.1 billion years after the Significant Bang. The discovery was published June 10 in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

It has been revealed that CRISTAL-02 is part of a larger sample of around two dozen star-forming galaxies at a similar distance (and therefore of a similar age). Observations revealed a huge plume of cold gas extending outside the galaxy, almost as large as the galaxy it comes from. The plume is moving toward Earth at some 60 miles (100 kilometers) per second. Finding fast-moving gas so far from the galaxy is a sign the gas is being actively pushed out in a wind-driven process.

But to truly determine the nature of the plume, the team first had to rule out another possibility behind its formation: Because CRISTAL-02 also appears to be in the throes of merging with several other galaxies, the plume could be a tidal tail — gas stripped away by gravitational forces during the interaction, rather than a genuine wind. This was tricky to determine, Davies claims, as no single measurement could settle the question of the gas’ origin; instead the team had to combine several different measurements to characterize the plume and confirm its cause.

Recent findings suggest that first, Davies’ team measured how many upcoming stars the galaxy produces each year. Massive stars live much shorter lives than less massive ones, so looking at how many young, massive stars are in a galaxy indicates how promptly it is forming new stars to replace the ones that are dying. So, the team searched for signs of these young, massive stars in the galaxy’s spectrum and measured how bright those features appear.

It has been revealed that the researchers also needed to determine how much gas the galaxy is losing. They did so by first using ALMA data to calculate the mass in the plume and then combining it with the gas’ velocity and distance from the galaxy’s center.

The verdict: CRISTAL-02 is forming stars at roughly three times the rate of a typical galaxy its size at this distance, but is losing twice as much gas as the galaxy’s star-formation rate. “If this rapid blowout continues, the galaxy could be dead in less than 50 million years, explaining the origin of the mysterious massive dead galaxies in the early universe,” Davies said in a press release.

Finally, the team turned to identifying the cause of the plume. Was the gas being pushed out by energy coming from the galaxy’s central black hole, or was the galaxy’s burst of intense star formation — and the resulting supernova blasts — the culprit?

Models predict that the most powerful outflows from massive galaxies like these should be the result of accretion onto supermassive black holes, Davies notes. But CRISTAL-02 shows no sign of AGN activity in its center. On the other hand, based on the amount of massive young stars in the galaxy, Davies’ team calculated that the energy transferred to the surrounding gas as these stars die and explode as supernovae would be powerful enough to produce the observed plume.

It has been revealed that the speed of the gas backs this idea up. Supernova-driven outflows rarely exceed speeds of about 1,550 miles (2,500 km) per second, states Christy Tremonti, an astronomer at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who was not involved in the study. Velocities higher than this usually point to an AGN as the energy source. CRISTAL-02’s outflow is moving around 400 miles (640 km) per second, comfortably within the range expected for a wind produced by a powerful starburst.

In a recent development, davies says that “the result is surprising,” going against the conventional wisdom that AGN are the cause of star-formation-ending winds. Tremonti notes that  “theoretical models love to use AGN feedback to shut off star formation in massive galaxies — almost every simulation does.” Yet CRISTAL-02’s star formation alone appears capable of triggering a wind that could exhaust its gas supply within tens of millions of years.

In a recent development, CRISTAL-02’s story may not be an isolated case, Davies indicates. Studies suggest that around 40% of massive star-forming galaxies in the early universe are merging, meaning many of them may be caught in similar growth spurts. If this commonly results in subsequent supernova-driven winds, it could help explain why so many early galaxies burned brightly and died young. “It may be the case that AGN are really important for keeping star formation off, but maybe they’re not the thing that shuts it down initially,” Tremonti says.

Recent findings suggest that the case isn’t entirely closed. Davies says her team cannot completely rule out the presence of an active supermassive black hole — either one too faint to detect, or one that may have flared briefly in the past and pushed gas away from the galaxy before subsequently fading from view. Tremonti agrees this is one of the hardest scenarios to eliminate. Future observations in the mid-infrared, which can peer through dust that might otherwise hide a buried black hole, could help close this gap.

As for CRISTAL-02, its fate is somewhat ironic: The explosive burst of star formation it is undergoing is also the underlying cause of its imminent death.

According to recent reports, shreejaya Karantha is a science writer based in India. Her work has appeared in Sky & Telescope, Phys.org, Live Science US, and The Hindu.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept.
  • Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.
  • Sources stated Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who currently serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept. 23. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.

Sources stated Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who currently serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget. The White House submitted ethics paperwork on Ueland — required for nominations — to the GAO, according to a source.

According to recent reports, senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., on Thursday posted notice of a committee hearing Nov. 19 to examine more than a dozen presidential nominees for executive and judicial offices, including “a nominee to be Comptroller General.”.

Recent findings suggest that the post identifies by name all of the nominees except the candidate for comptroller general. The post has been filled by an acting comptroller general, Orice Williams Brown, since Gene L. Dodaro completed his 15-year term at the end of last year.

The move by Paul to short-circuit the convening of a legislative commission to recommend candidates infuriated top Democrats, who excoriated the chairman in a joint statement Wednesday night. A special bipartisan, bicameral legislative commission is supposed to recommend at least three candidates for comptroller general to the president, according to statute.

Homeland Security Committee GOP staff solicited recommendations for a comptroller general from some Democratic congressional offices Wednesday afternoon, imposing a deadline of 8 a.m. Thursday, according to Democratic aides.

The president nominates the head of the GAO, the investigative arm of Congress, with the advice and consent of the Senate.

Paul pushed back on the criticism Thursday, saying, “Democrats have known about this for months and months and months.” He mentioned the last time the special commission made recommendations for the office, when Barack Obama was president, “Democrats submitted their own list, Republicans submitted their own list. So they can complain all they want but they just need to make their list and submit it.”.

In the past, however, the special commission convened, sought applications for the position, interviewed candidates and deliberated before sending recommendations to the president.

A 1980 law states that when there is a vacancy in the comptroller general position, “there is established a commission to recommend individuals to the President for appointment to the vacant office,” and that the commission must submit at least three names.

Under the statute, the commission includes the speaker, Senate majority and minority leaders, House majority and minority leaders, chairs and ranking members of the Senate Homeland Security and House Oversight and Government Reform committees, and the Senate president pro tempore.

In a recent development, in 1981, for example, after the law took effect, the two congressional leaders, Speaker Thomas P. “Tip” O’Neill Jr., D-Mass., and Senate Majority Leader Howard H. Baker, R-Tenn., sent a letter to President Ronald Reagan saying the special commission had met and voted to recommend eight candidates to succeed Comptroller General Elmer Staats.

“The members of the Commission have taken their statutory responsibility seriously,” they wrote.

Recent findings suggest that reagan nominated Charles A. Bowsher, who was on the list, and he was confirmed.

Sources indicate that after Bowsher’s term ended in 1996, the commission eventually formed, interviewed multiple candidates, and deliberated for several months. Republicans controlled both chambers, and Bill Clinton was president. The members of the commission could not reach agreement, and as a result, the Republicans on the committee submitted their list to Clinton, and the Democrats on the panel submitted theirs.

Clinton also had his own list. Clinton nominated David M. Walker, who was on all three lists, and he was confirmed by the Senate more than two years after Bowsher’s departure. Walker argued Thursday against short-circuiting the commission process.

Recent findings suggest that “The position is of critical importance and the related statutory Commission process should not be circumvented," Walker said. "Doing so would undercut the credibility of the person and the effectiveness of the GAO.”.

Walker resigned in March of 2008, when George W. Bush was still president. He appointed Dodaro as acting comptroller general when he left. The commission got going several months later, creating a website with application instructions and candidate questions.

Over the next two years, the commission interviewed some 20 candidates. Democrats and Republicans on the panel were unable to reach agreement, and Democrats, who had a majority on the commission, submitted their own list to Obama in 2010. Republicans followed up with their list.

“The Commission has been working in earnest on this undertaking for more than one year and has dedicated considerable time and effort to present you with highly qualified candidates for this important position,” then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., along with other Democratic leaders, wrote to Obama when they submitted the Democrats’ list.

The Democrats’ move drew a rebuke from Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who was ranking member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee at the time.

Collins said in a statement she was “extremely disappointed” that Democrats “abruptly ended the selection process for the next Comptroller General without a bipartisan agreement” on the recommendations. “We have had several exceptionally qualified individuals apply to be the next leader of the GAO, and it should have been possible to come up with a consensus list.”.

Obama nominated and the Senate confirmed Dodaro, who was one of four recommendations from the Democrats.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A management researcher scored a 1629 mutiny leader against a modern corporate psychopath checklist, and he matched all ten traits.

For about 30 years, researchers have studied corporate psychopaths. They are the charming, ruthless bosses who rule by fear and blame everyone else. Most of the examples that come to mind are usually living or recent executives.

Now the earliest one on record may be a merchant who ran a survivors’ camp after a 1629 wreck. Scored against a ten-item checklist built for today’s boardrooms, Jeronimus Cornelisz of the Dutch East India Firm matches every item.

Industry observers note that clive Boddy, an associate professor of management at Anglia Ruskin University in England, wrote the paper alone. Boddy has spent years studying corporate psychopathy.

This paper is a historical case study rather than an experiment. It leans mainly on the historian Mike Dash’s 2003 book about the wreck.

Other sources are the expedition commander’s journal, a pastor’s letters, trial records, and skeletons dug up on the island.

“What makes this case remarkable is that when we analyzed Cornelisz using a modern management psychopathy framework, he displayed every major characteristic associated with corporate psychopaths,” Boddy stated.

The Batavia was the company’s latest flagship, bound for the port the Dutch had renamed Batavia, now Jakarta.

On the morning of June 4, 1629, it struck a reef in the Houtman Abrolhos islands. The reef lies 80 miles (130 kilometers) off Western Australia, and most of the people aboard managed to reach a small coral island.

Recent findings suggest that somewhere between 180 and 250 people made it ashore, and 30 of them were women and children. The island had no fresh water of its own.

The commander, Francisco Pelsaert, the ship’s captain, and 46 others then left in an overloaded longboat to fetch help from Jakarta, 900 miles (1,450 kilometers) away.

That left Cornelisz, a junior merchant and the most senior tech giant man still on the island, in charge of everyone else.

According to recent reports, cornelisz had been plotting a mutiny before the ship went down. Once in command, Boddy wrote, he replaced the lawful council with his fellow plotters and had them swear personal oaths of loyalty.

He moved the money chests, water, and food into his own tent, and the initiative was to seize whatever rescue ship arrived and turn pirate.

According to recent reports, he also sent groups of survivors to two other islands, supposedly to look for water, and left them there. Then he told his followers that the island’s population had to shrink if supplies were to last.

Between 96 and 115 men, women, and children were murdered over the following weeks, and some of the women were subjected to sexual violence.

It has been revealed that cornelisz ordered the killings and, with one exception, left others to carry them out. A pastor who survived wrote that the remaining people lived in constant fear of being next.

In Boddy’s reading, that climate of fear is the same tool corporate psychopaths use to keep a workforce in line.

The soldiers Cornelisz had dumped on the farthest island did not die. Their island had two freshwater wells, seabird colonies, fish, wallabies, and seals.

Under a soldier named Wiebbe Hayes, the group of 46 men and a boy fed itself and took in people who escaped the killings.

When word of the murders reached them, Hayes had his men forge pikes from wreckage, pile up coral to throw, and build a small stone fort on a hill.

Recent findings suggest that they turned back two raids, captured Cornelisz during a third attempt, and were holding off a fourth, this time against muskets, when the rescue ship appeared. Hayes’s men reached it first and warned the crew.

Cornelisz and his ringleaders were tried on the spot, confessed, and were hanged. Hayes was promoted.

Boddy calls the two islands a natural experiment in leadership: same wreck, same weather, and one group built cooperation and found food while the other descended into murder.

The checklist is a ten-item measure of what researchers call primary psychopathy, written for management research rather than for prisons.

Boddy’s rule for judging someone from history is that they must clearly show at least eight of the ten. The same test has been applied to the financier Bernard Madoff, the media owner Robert Maxwell, and the Nazi leader Hermann Goering.

It has been revealed that cornelisz scores on all ten in the paper’s table of characteristics shown by corporate psychopaths. The items include superficial charm, habitual lying, total self-regard, no remorse, and shallow emotion.

It has been revealed that they end with a calm, rational manner while ordering murders, and no insight into his own behavior. Dash had already called Cornelisz a psychopath on an informal reading of the criminal criteria.

It has been revealed that boddy’s paper is the first to run him through a management measure item by item. The record it draws on includes the wreck itself, found by divers in 1963 and partly reconstructed by the Western Australian Museum.

Boddy also visited the Museum of Geraldton, which holds finds from the wreck, as background.

Everything in the assessment comes from documents and from one historian’s account of them. There is no way to interview, test, or observe the man himself, and the paper reports no new data and has no limitations section of its own.

Prevalence is the other open number. About 1 percent of adults are usually counted as categorically psychopathic, and a newer pooled analysis that used non-criminal measures found 4.5 percent. Either way, the share is small in the general population.

Sources indicate that among senior corporate leaders, one estimate comes to about 4 percent, with some industries drawing more of the money-hungry personality than others. How many of them run companies today isn’t something a shipwreck from 1629 can say.

Boddy’s next candidate is another organization man, Governor General Jan Coen, who ordered massacres while building the Dutch spice monopoly.

It has been revealed that the paper closes by asking personnel departments to weigh character and values when they pick senior leaders. The pattern it describes, Boddy wrote, has apparently been in place since the first shareholder-owned company existed.

The full study was published in the journal Asian Journal of Business Ethics.

Motion under the ocean explains the depth of the world’s deepest spot

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (642 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Challenger Deep is the deepest valley in the deepest trench in the ocean, plunging to roughly 11,000 meters below sea level.
  • Now, scientists have a new clue about how it got to be so … well, deep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Challenger Deep is the deepest valley in the deepest trench in the ocean, plunging to roughly 11,000 meters below sea level.

Now, scientists have a new clue about how it got to be so … well, deep.

In a recent development, challenger Deep is found within the Mariana Trench, a crescent-shaped gouge in the seafloor east of the Philippines in the Pacific Ocean. The trench is the scene of a slo-mo tectonic collision called a subduction zone: The Pacific plate is diving beneath the Mariana plate, bending downward as it sinks into the mantle, forming a steep trench on the ocean floor.

All subduction zones are deep, but “it’s interesting why this is the deepest spot in the Earth’s ocean,” states geoscientist Robert Stern, an emeritus professor at the University of Texas at Dallas and a visiting researcher at the University of California, Los Angeles.

He and colleagues employed a remotely operated robot called ROV Jason/Medea to descend to more than 6,000 meters and explore the Mariana Trench seafloor around the edges of Challenger Deep. The rocks turned out to contain pyroclastic deposits, evidence of an erstwhile explosive volcanic eruption. Those deposits included platelike blocks that could indicate eruption pulses, and lobe-shaped rocks where the volcanic flows ended and quickly cooled.

These are the deepest pyroclastic deposits found on Earth, the scientists report November 23 in Frontiers in Earth Science.

How explosive an eruption is at Earth’s surface depends on the chemical makeup of the magma. When the molten rock contains a high proportion of volatile gases, including water vapor, those gases suddenly expand when the magma reaches the surface, producing a violent explosion.

Such explosive volcanism shouldn’t be possible in the deep sea; the pressure is too high for any escaping gases to expand, Stern indicates. Along with that mystery, the volcanic deposits were found unusually close to the trench, compared with what would be expected for a subduction zone.

Stern and his colleagues developed a hypothesis that incorporates these disparate pieces of evidence: The extreme depth of Challenger Deep, they say, may be at least partially due to an especially sharp bend in the Pacific Plate as it sinks into the mantle.

That tighter bend would explain why volcanism is happening closer to the subduction zone than usual. The classic subduction zone scenario is that the sinking plate heats up and melts partially as it descends; the magma rises through the overhanging plate and erupts, forming volcanic island arcs several hundred kilometers from the collision zone. Here, the volcanic deposits were just a hundred kilometers or so from the trench — which makes sense if the plate is dipping more steeply.

In a recent development, as for the pyroclastics, “we can’t answer if the eruptions were really explosive,” Stern claims. But at those pressures, any gases such as water vapor contained in the magma wouldn’t be able to explosively expand as they would at the surface.

It has been revealed that instead, the pyroclastic rocks might have formed through a new version of deep-sea eruption, one in which water emerging from the magma is initially in a supercritical fluid state. That would minimize any explosive expansion during the eruption and could also produce fragmented, dense deposits like those seen by Jason/Medea.

The discovery of deep-sea pyroclastics is “surprising and unprecedented,” says William Chadwick, a geologist at Oregon State University in Newport. Challenger Deep may be the only place on Earth “with the ingredients to produce explosive volcanism in the super-deep ocean,” he says. “Imagining this happening is … pretty mind-boggling.”.

A lot more work remains to be done to evaluate all of these fresh ideas, Stern notes. “But a lot of things are now coming together.”.

Phaethon’s fiery folly

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (405 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, even the best-laid prepares can require a bit of luck to execute.
  • According to recent reports, “I deliberately positioned myself near a local airport in the hope that an aircraft might cross the Sun during the eclipse,” he tells Astronomy.
  • It has been revealed that the work wasn’t over: The image “required a somewhat more elaborate workflow” than the conventional stacking and sharpening of video frames.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, even the best-laid prepares can require a bit of luck to execute. During the solar eclipse of Aug. 12, 2026, in which parts of Iceland, Portugal, and Spain experienced totality, much of western Europe enjoyed a substantial partial eclipse. Astrophotographer Alexandre Tournay set up near Brussels to capture the Moon crossing the disk — as well as a transit of another kind.

According to recent reports, “I deliberately positioned myself near a local airport in the hope that an aircraft might cross the Sun during the eclipse,” he tells Astronomy. “Against the odds, one did, passing across the partially eclipsed solar disk with its contrail trailing behind it.” Flight tracking data allowed him to pinpoint the flight: Cargolux 5933, a Boeing 747 freighter from Mexico City bound for Luxembourg.

It has been revealed that the work wasn’t over: The image “required a somewhat more elaborate workflow” than the conventional stacking and sharpening of video frames. That process brings out the roiling details in the Sun’s chromosphere, but would oversharpen the edges of the airplane and Moon. So Tournay blended a 1,000-frame stack of the Sun with a single frame that preserved the silhouettes and froze their motion against the disk.

He named the resulting image “Phaethon’s Flight” after the boy in Greek mythology who journeyed east to prove that his father was Helios, the Sun god. Phaethon convinced Helios to let him drive his Sun-bearing chariot across the sky, but was unable to control the horses. He blazed an erratic path that brought climatic extremes to Earth — freezing cold and scorching heat — before Zeus intervened and struck him down dead.

According to recent reports, “There’s something fascinating about being able to photograph, with modern instruments, a celestial phenomenon that our ancestors could only understand and describe through mythology,” notes Tournay. “And then, by pure chance, to have a flying machine cross the Sun at that exact moment, almost as though a modern-day chariot were dragging the eclipse behind it across the sky, made the story of Phaethon feel like a perfect fit. Seeing that plane cross the eclipsed Sun, I can almost hear the ancients screaming, ‘See?! I told you it was Phaethon!’ ”.

Mark Zastrow is Editor-in-Chief of Astronomy magazine. He holds masters degrees in astronomy and science journalism and has over a decade of experience covering science in the U.S. and in Asia.

#122998. Latest Update: Northern ice sheets may have cooled the deep ocean and pulled carbon from the air, causing the last Ice Age

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1106 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Northern ice sheets may have cooled the deep ocean and pulled carbon from the air, causing the last Ice Age

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1106 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A simplified ocean model indicates cooling only the far north drew nearly as much ice age carbon into the sea as cooling the whole planet.
  • The ice ages are known for the ice sheets that spread across the far north.
  • According to recent reports, A new modeling study suggests the two ends were connected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A simplified ocean model indicates cooling only the far north drew nearly as much ice age carbon into the sea as cooling the whole planet.

The ice ages are known for the ice sheets that spread across the far north. But much of an ice age’s cold came from carbon dioxide leaving the air. That carbon went into the ocean largely at the other end of the planet, around Antarctica.

According to recent reports, A new modeling study suggests the two ends were connected. Cooling only the ocean’s far north pulled nearly three-quarters as much CO2 out of the air as cooling the entire planet.

Madison Shankle of the University of St Andrews led the work with colleagues at the National Oceanography Centre and the University of Chicago.

In a recent development, the test ran in a simplified computer model of the ocean with no real ice sheet in it. So the result is a mechanism, not a measurement of the past.

Shankle remarked the team had “produced evidence of a plausible mechanism” linking the northern ice sheets to the changes around Antarctica that pulled CO2 from the air.

“Our study takes the step of actually demonstrating them working in model simulations, which is a major step forward for this field,” Shankle added.

It has been revealed that ice ages are paced by slow wobbles in Earth’s orbit, which change how much summer sunlight reaches the far north. Less summer sun lets ice sheets grow there.

However, the wobbles alone can’t make the planet as cold as it got. And the deep ocean is the only store big enough to hold the missing carbon.

In a recent development, much of the deep ocean’s water last touched the air in the Southern Ocean around Antarctica. This is where scientists have looked for the carbon.

According to recent reports, antarctic ice cores show that sea ice there grew and shrank in step with the northern ice sheets,. It did not change with the sunlight over Antarctica itself.

It has been revealed that in 2001, two researchers proposed an answer. Cold water sinks in the North Atlantic and flows south through the deep ocean.

If a northern ice sheet chilled that water, the chill would eventually arrive around Antarctica. This would cause sea ice to grow there, and set off the changes that store carbon.

Shankle’s team tested the idea in the MITgcm ocean model. The model ocean is one basin, 2.5 miles (4 kilometers) deep. It has a flat floor and runs from 70 degrees south to 70 degrees north.

Recent findings suggest that air temperatures over it are fixed, so it can’t grow an ice sheet,. The team cooled the air to stand in for one.

Recent findings suggest that the team ran four versions. One had warm, preindustrial-style air everywhere, and one was ice-age cold everywhere, 3.6°F (2°C) cooler at the equator and 10.8°F (6°C) cooler at the poles.

The other two cooled only the air north of 40.5 degrees north, either halfway to ice-age temperatures or all the way.

The cooled band is where northern water sinks to the deep, and it is small. It covers just 13 percent of the model’s surface. Each run lasted 15,000 model years, long enough for the deep ocean to settle.

Sources indicate that cooling the north cooled the whole model ocean. The biggest temperature drop was at mid-depths of 3,300 to 6,600 feet (1,000 to 2,000 meters). In the fully cooled northern run, that layer ended up colder than under global cooling.

It has been revealed that the far north turned out to have outsized reach. In the full northern run, the whole ocean cooled by 4.5°F (2.5°C) on average. An earlier run that applied the same cooling to the far south instead cooled the whole ocean by only 1.1°F (0.6°C).

The cold water grew sea ice around the model’s Antarctica, and ice thickness south of 60 degrees south roughly doubled in the half-cooled run and tripled in the full one.

It has been revealed that thicker ice leaves more salt behind when it freezes, so the bottom water got saltier and the deep ocean separated into more distinct layers. Records of the real ice ages show both features.

It has been revealed that atmospheric CO2 in the model fell by 14 parts per million with the half-cooled north, and 32 ppm with the fully cooled one. Cooling the whole planet brought it down 43 ppm. So the north alone produced 74 percent of the drawdown.

Most of that came from a simple fact: cold water holds more carbon dioxide.

Because the northern cooling reached the whole deep ocean, the extra carbon that the colder water absorbed matched or exceeded the global-cooling run.

The thicker Antarctic sea ice added more by capping water before it could give its carbon back to the air, at about half the strength of the global run.

Marine life worked against the storage: the cooler, more layered ocean left more nutrients unused at the surface, which released some carbon rather than storing it.

The real ice ages had iron-rich dust and shifting winds that fed ocean life, and the model has neither.

Air trapped in ice cores reveals CO2 fell from about 280 ppm to about 180 ppm, and the model wasn’t built to match that.

A 2022 study cooled the North Atlantic in a more realistic two-basin model and saw CO2 rise by 6 ppm instead. Its Atlantic current strengthened and brought deep carbon back toward the surface.

Recent findings suggest that in that model, the deep water started out warmer, about 43°F to 46°F (6°C to 8°C) against 36°F to 39°F (2°C to 4°C) in the fresh one. It may not have cooled enough to grow southern sea ice, Shankle’s team wrote.

The newly introduced model has limits of its own. It has a flat floor, no real ice sheet, no changing winds, and no seasons, and its CO2 doesn’t warm or cool the air.

The air over its Antarctica also stayed at warm, preindustrial temperatures, which probably held back the sea ice and understated the effect, the authors wrote.

Whether a real ice sheet, with its winds and seasons, could set off the same chain in the real Southern Ocean is the open question. The team’s next step is a model with a growing ice sheet built in, and they want the idea tested in fuller models of the Earth.

The full study was published in the Journal of Climate.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 24: A Super Beaver Moon occults the Pleiades.

Sources indicate that the distant ice giant Uranus reaches opposition tonight at 6 P.M. EST. Opposition is the best time to view a planet in our sky, and it’s visible roughly from dusk until dawn. Because Uranus is faint — magnitude 5.6 — you’ll want to give it a few hours after sunset to climb away from both light pollution and turbulent air near the horizon. Around 10 P.M. local time, you’ll find Uranus midway between the bright star Aldebaran and the Pleiades star cluster in Taurus the Bull, about 60° above the southeastern horizon. It sits some 1.5° south of 4th-magnitude 37 Tauri.

Although Uranus can be visible to the naked eye under clear, dark conditions, the bright waning Moon is nearby, so pull out binoculars or a telescope to view the far-off planet tonight. Once you land on its location, look for a “flat,” grayish-colored star. Uranus’ disk spans 4”, so you will likely be able to tell it is circular, rather than a pinpoint of light like any background stars.
